His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts? Are they then the victors?﴾.

Regarding the meaning of Allah's coming to the land, reducing it from its outskirts, in this noble verse, there are well-known opinions among the scholars, some of which are supported by a Qur'anic indication.

Some scholars said: its reduction from its outskirts is the death of the scholars. A *marfu'* (a hadith traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) has been reported on this from Abu Hurayrah. But the distance of this view from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, according to the indication of the context, is evident, as you see.

Some people of knowledge said: its reduction from its outskirts is its ruin at the death of its people.

Some people of knowledge said: its reduction from its outskirts is the reduction of souls and fruits, and other opinions. As for the view indicated by the Qur'anic clue, it is that the meaning of ﴿We reduce it from its outskirts﴾ is: We reduce the land of disbelief and the abode of war, and We remove its outskirts by empowering the Muslims over it, giving them victory over its people, and returning it to the abode of Islam. The clue indicating this meaning is His saying after it: ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44]. The interrogation is for denying their victory. It was also said: it is for affirming that they are defeated, not victorious. So His saying "Are they then the victors?" is evidence that the reduction of the land from its outskirts is a cause for the victory of the Muslims over the disbelievers, and this only occurs in the sense mentioned. Among what supports this interpretation is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done, or it will settle near their homes, until the promise of Allah comes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], according to the view of one who said that the disaster that strikes them is the expeditions of the Prophet ﷺ, which conquer the outskirts of their lands, or that you, O Prophet of Allah, will settle near their homes. Among those from whom this view is related are Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, and others. This meaning which Allah mentions here He also mentions at the end of surah "al-Ra'd," in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse of "al-Anbiya'": the best explanation of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have destroyed what is around you of the cities, and We have varied the signs so that they may return﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27].

The one who restricts this (i.e., the author of this commentary), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What Ibn Kathir mentioned is correct, and the inductive study of the Great Qur'an indicates it. Accordingly, the meaning is: Do not the disbelievers of Makkah, and whoever follows their course in denying you, O Prophet of Allah, and in disbelieving what you have brought, see ﴿that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts﴾? That is, by destroying those who denied the messengers, as We destroyed the people of Salih and the people of Lut, while they pass by their dwellings, and as We destroyed the people of Hud, and made Saba' into tales and scattered them completely. All of that was because of denying the messengers and disbelieving what they brought. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We have destroyed what is around you of the cities﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27], such as the people of Salih, the people of Lut, the people of Hud, and Saba'. So beware of denying our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, lest We bring down upon you the like of what We brought down upon them. This view does not conflict with His saying after it: ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾, and the meaning is that victory belongs to the party of Allah, the One capable of all things, who destroyed what is around you of the cities because of their denying their messengers. You are not stronger than them, nor greater in wealth or children, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Are they better than the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37], and the verse. And Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in traces left upon the earth, but what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ [Ghafir: 82]. And Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them, and they stirred up the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it﴾, the verse [al-Rum: 9], and other verses.

The warning to those who denied him ﷺ by what befell those who denied the messengers before him is very frequent in the Qur'an. And by this you know the direction of what Ibn Kathir found good, of interpreting this verse of "al-Anbiya'" by the verse of "al-Ahqaf" mentioned, as we have explained.

Al-Zamakhshari said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿We come to the land﴾? I say: In it is a depiction of what Allah was bringing about at the hands of the Muslims, and that their armies and expeditions were raiding the land of the polytheists, coming to it as victors over it, having reduced it from its outskirts." End of his quotation. And Allah, may He be exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 47:

The Qur'anic text: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. Even if it is the weight of a grain of mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners.﴾

He, exalted and majestic, mentions in this noble verse that He sets up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, and their deeds are weighed with the utmost justice and fairness. Allah does not wrong anyone in the least. Even if a person's deed, whether good or bad, is of the utmost smallness and fineness, like the weight of a grain of mustard seed, Allah will bring it forth, because nothing is hidden from Him. And He, exalted and majestic, is sufficient as a reckoner, because His knowledge encompasses everything.

In another place He explains that, at that weighing, the scales are of two kinds: some are light and some are heavy. Whoever's scales are light is destroyed, and whoever's scales are heavy is saved. As in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. Those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs.﴾ [al-A'raf: 8–9]

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another. Those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding forever in Hell.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101–103]

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his mother will be the Abyss.﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 6–9]

And other verses besides these.

As for what He, exalted and majestic, mentions in this noble verse, that the scales of the Day of Resurrection are scales of justice, He mentioned it in al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 8], because the truth is justice and equity. And what He mentions in it, that no soul will be wronged in the least, He has clarified in many other places, such as His saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom. And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but it is people who wrong themselves.﴾ [Yunus: 44]

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone.﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]

We have already presented the verses that indicate this in surah al-Kahf.

As for what He, exalted and majestic, mentions in this noble verse, that a deed, even if it is the weight of an atom of good or evil that He has brought, He has clarified in another place, as in His saying about Luqman, affirming it for him: ﴿O my son, indeed, if it is the weight of a grain of mustard seed and is within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted.﴾ [Luqman: 16]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7–8], and other verses besides these.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And We shall set up the scales﴾, "mawazin" is the plural of "mizan" (scale). The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that each person has multiple scales, by His saying: ﴿Those whose scales are heavy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 102] and His saying: ﴿And those whose scales are light﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 103]. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that a single doer has several scales, and with each one a category of his deeds is weighed, as the poet said:

A king, for whose justice the calamities stand, so for every calamity there is a scale for it.

The established rule in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the science of legal theory) is that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an may not be departed from except by a proof that must be followed. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "Most scholars hold that it is only one scale, and it is pluralized only in consideration of the multiplicity of the deeds weighed in it." We have already presented, at the end of surah al-Kahf, the words of the scholars on how deeds are weighed, which makes repeating it here unnecessary.

His saying in this verse: "al-qist" means justice. It is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive, and for this reason it is kept in the singular form, as he said in the Khulasa (Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik):

And they described with the verbal noun often, so they kept it singular and masculine.

As we have presented many times before. It is known that describing with a verbal noun, some scholars say it is for emphasis (mubalaghah). Others say it is by the implied structure of an omitted genitive (mudaf mahdhuf), meaning "scales possessing justice." According to the first view, it is as if the scales are emphasized in their justice so much that they are called "al-qist," which is justice. According to the second view, the meaning is: scales possessing justice.

The lam in His saying ﴿li-yawm al-qiyamah﴾ ("for the Day of Resurrection") has well-known interpretations among the scholars:

(Among them): that it is for specifying time, i.e., indicating a time, as the Arabs say: "I came five nights before the end of the month." And from this is the saying of Nabigha Dhubyani:

I recognized the traces of her (dwelling), after six years, and this year is the seventh.

(Among them): that it is the lam of purpose (kay), meaning: We set up the scales of justice for the sake of the Day of Resurrection, i.e., for the reckoning of people on it, a reckoning of the utmost justice and fairness.

(Among them): that it means "in" (fi), i.e., We set up the scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection.

The Kufans say that the lam comes in the sense of "in" (fi), and they say that among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47], meaning "in the Day of Resurrection", and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], meaning "at its time". Ibn Qutaybah among the earlier scholars agreed with them in this, and Ibn Malik among the later scholars did too, and he recited as evidence the verse of Miskin al-Darimi:

Those are my people, who have passed on their way, as 'Ad and Tubba' passed before them.

meaning, "they passed in their way." And the saying of another:

Every father and son, even if they lived long together, both residing, one is lost for a time and one is missing.

meaning "in a time."

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿So no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ may be that "shay'an" (in the least) is the second object of "tuzlamu" (is wronged), and it may be that it substitutes for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). That is: "any amount of wrong, not a little nor a lot."

"Mithqal al-shay'" is its weight. "Al-khardal" is a seed of the utmost smallness and fineness. Some people of knowledge say it is the seed of the wild rocket (zari'at al-jirjir). The pronoun in His saying "bi-ha" (by it) is feminine, though it refers to the construct "mithqal," which is masculine, because it has acquired the feminine gender from the genitive that follows it, which is ﴿grain of mustard seed﴾, in the manner of his saying in the Khulasa:

Sometimes the second word confers feminine gender on the first, if the first is capable of having an omission.

A similar usage in the speech of the Arabs is the saying of 'Antarah in his Mu'allaqah:

Every abundant eye poured over him, so they left every hollow like a dirham.

And the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

The length of nights hastened to wear me down, they wore out all of me and wore out part of me.

And the saying of al-A'sha:

And it blazes with the word that I have spread, as the spearhead's bloodied edge blazes with blood.

And the saying of another:

They walked as spears sway when their upper parts have been made light by the blowing of the gusty winds.

In the first verse he made the word "kull" (every) feminine because it is attached to "'ayn" (eye). In the second verse he made "tul" (length) feminine because it is attached to "al-layali" (the nights). In the third verse he made "al-sadr" (the breast/edge) feminine because it is attached to "al-qanah" (the spear). In the fourth verse he made "marr" (passing) feminine because it is attached to "al-riyah" (the winds). The genitive constructs mentioned, if omitted, would leave the sentence sound, as he said in the Khulasa:

. . . . . . . . . if it is capable of omission.

This letter was read by all the readers except Nafi': ﴿wa-in kana mithqala habbah﴾ with the accusative on "mithqal," as the predicate of "kana" (was), meaning: "and if the deed to be weighed is the weight of a grain of mustard seed."

Nafi' alone read ﴿wa-in kana mithqalu﴾ with the nominative, as the subject of "kana," considering it a complete verb (taammah), like His saying: ﴿and if there is one in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder that We have sent down. Will you then deny it?﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that this great Qur'an is ﴿a blessed reminder﴾, meaning abundant in blessings and goodness, because in it is the good of this world and the Hereafter. Then He rebukes those who deny it, censuring them with His saying: ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾

What He, majestic and exalted, mentions in this noble verse, that this Qur'an is blessed (p-162), He explains in several places in His Book, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He, in "al-An'am" (The Cattle): ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 155]

• And His saying in the same surah: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what was before it﴾ [al-An'am: 92]

• And His saying, exalted is He, in "Sad": ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad: 29]

and other verses besides these. So we ask God, the Near, the Responsive, that the blessings of this great and blessed Book overwhelm us, by God's granting us success to reflect upon its verses and to act upon what it contains of the lawful and the unlawful, its commands and prohibitions, its noble qualities and its etiquettes, in compliance and in abstention. Indeed He is Near and Responsive.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment before, and We were of him well-acquainted.﴾

We have already presented, in surah Maryam, what clarifies these verses up to the end of the story in the Qur'an, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Burn him, and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾

In this noble verse, He - exalted and majestic is He - mentions that when His prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him and upon our Prophet) overwhelmed his disbelieving people with clear proofs and decisive arguments, they resorted to the use of force. They said: ﴿Burn him, and support your gods, if you are going to act﴾ [al-Anbiya': 68], meaning: by killing the enemy of your gods, Ibrahim, in the worst way of killing, which is burning with fire.

It is not mentioned here that they intended to kill him by other than burning, but He, exalted is He, mentioned in surah al-'Ankabut that they ﴿said: "Kill him or burn him"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24], in His saying: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Kill him or burn him."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24].

It is a custom that when the one in falsehood is overwhelmed by evidence, he resorts to whatever power he has in order to use it against the truth.

As for His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿if you are going to act﴾, meaning: if you are going to support your gods with a strong support, then choose for him the most grievous kind of killing, which is burning with fire; otherwise you will have fallen short in supporting them.

(p-163) The phrase "Say: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim" (﴿قُلْنا يا نارُ كُونِي بَرْدًا وسَلاما عَلى إبْراهِيمَ﴾) and what follows, "they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers" (﴿وأرادُوا بِهِ كَيْدًا فَجَعَلْناهُمُ الأخْسَرِينَ﴾), contain an ellipsis that the context makes clear. Its implied sense is: they said, "Burn him," and they threw him into the fire. When they had done that, [God] said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety﴾. The matter has been explained in Surat al-Saffat, where it is stated that when they wanted to throw him into the fire, they built a structure for him so that they could cast him into it.

According to the narrative, they threw him from that high structure by catapult (al-manjaniq), at the indication of a man from the Arabs of Persia (meaning the Kurds). God caused the earth to swallow him, and he is still sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection. God says: ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire"﴾ [al-Saffat: 97]. The exegetes mention the great intensity of this fire, the height of its flames, and the abundance of its fuel, which were something tremendous and awesome. They also report, concerning the Prophet of God, Ibrahim, that when they bound him, stripped of his clothing, and threw him toward the fire, Gabriel said to him, "Do you have any need?" He said, "As for you, no. As for God, yes, indeed." [Gabriel] said, "Then why do you not ask Him?" He said, "His knowledge of my condition is sufficient for me, in place of my asking."

What God, may He be exalted, mentions in this noble verse, namely that He commanded the fire, by His universal and decreed command, to be coolness and safety for Ibrahim, indicates that He delivered him from that fire. This is because His saying, ﴿be coolness﴾ [21], indicates his safety from its heat, and His saying "and safety" indicates his safety from the evil of the coldness into which the heat was transformed. His rescuing him from it, which is indicated here by His decreed universal command, is stated explicitly in al-'Ankabut in His saying: ﴿So God rescued him from the fire﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24]. He alluded to this here by His saying: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot﴾ [al-Anbiya': 71].

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 70], it is clarified by what precedes it. The scheme they intended against him was to burn him with fire, as a means of victory for their gods, in their supposition. His making them, may He be exalted, "the greatest losers," meaning those who suffered the greatest loss, is due to the failure of their scheme and his safety from their fire.

God has also alluded to this in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿So they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the lowest﴾ [al-Saffat: 98]. That they were "the lowest" is clear, since he was exalted above them and safe from their evil. That they were "the greatest losers" is because they lost both this world and the Hereafter; that is the manifest loss. The narrative also states that God sent against them a creature of His weakest creatures, and it destroyed them, namely the gnat. It is also related in the narrative that all beasts extinguished the fire for Ibrahim, except the gecko (al-wazagh), which blew upon the fire against him. We have already presented the hadiths that command the killing of geckos in Surat al-An'am.

It is reported from Abu al-'Aliyah: "Had God not said, 'and safety,' its coldness would have been more harmful to him than its heat. Had He not said, 'upon Ibrahim,' its coldness would have remained forever." It is reported from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that: "Had He not said, 'and safety,' Ibrahim would have died from its coldness." It is reported from al-Suddi: "On that day no fire remained anywhere but was extinguished." It is reported from Ka'b and Qatadah: "The fire burned nothing of Ibrahim except his bonds." It is reported from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr: Ibrahim said, "I never had days more blessed than the days I spent in the fire." It is reported from Shu'ayb al-Himmani that he was thrown into the fire when he was sixteen years old. It is reported from Ibn Jurayj: he was thrown into it when he was twenty-six. It is reported from al-Kalbi: "The fires of the whole earth became cool, and that day it did not cook a single shank."

They also mention in the narrative that Nimrod looked down at the fire from the palace (al-sarh), and saw Ibrahim sitting on a throne, being kept company by the angel of the shade. He said, "How excellent is your Lord! I will surely offer to Him four thousand cows," and he desisted from him. All of this is from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives derived from Jewish and Christian sources). The exegetes mention much of these in this story and in other stories of the prophets.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us, I think he said: Abu Bakr narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Abu al-Duha, from Ibn 'Abbas: 'Hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil' ('God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs'), which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said when he was thrown into the fire, and which Muhammad (ﷺ) said when they said: ﴿Those to whom the people said, 'Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them,' but it increased them in faith and they said, 'God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs'﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]." Malik ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Abu al-Duha, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The last words of Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire were: 'Hasbiya Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil.'" End.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 71:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds﴾.

The pronoun in His saying "and We delivered him" refers to Ibrahim. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit: "The phrase 'and We delivered him' has been given the meaning of 'We brought him out, by Our deliverance, to the land.' For this reason 'najjaynahu' (delivered him) takes 'ila' (to). It is possible that 'ila' is connected to an omitted element, meaning 'reaching to the land,' in which case it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and on this reading there is no implicit extension of meaning in 'najjaynahu.' The land from which they departed is Kutha in the land of Iraq, and the land to which they departed is the land of al-Sham." End of quotation from him. This noble verse alludes to the migration of Ibrahim, with Lot accompanying him, from the land of Iraq to al-Sham, fleeing with their religion.

Allah, exalted is He, has indicated this in another place:

• As in His saying in "al-'Ankabut": ﴿So Lot believed in him, and he said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26]

• And His saying in "as-Saffat": ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [as-Saffat: 99], according to the more apparent of the two opinions, because he was fleeing with his religion to his Lord away from the disbelievers. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of His saying, "And he said, 'Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me'": this verse is the basis for migration and seclusion, and the first to do so was Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when Allah rescued him from the fire. He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord," meaning: I am migrating from the land of my people and my birthplace to where I can worship my Lord, "for He will guide me," in what I intend, to what is right. As for what He, exalted and majestic, indicated, that He blessed for the worlds the aforementioned land, which is al-Sham, according to the opinion of the majority regarding this verse,

• by His saying: ﴿to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 71], He clarified it in another place,

• as in His saying: ﴿And to Solomon the wind, blowing forcefully by his command toward the land which We had blessed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 81],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. The meaning of His having blessed it ("baraka fiha") is what He placed in it of fertility, trees, rivers, and fruits, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And had the people of the cities believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96].

Among that is that He sent most of the prophets from it.

Some scholars of knowledge said: Among that is that the source of every sweet water is from beneath the rock that is near Bayt al-Maqdis. A hadith marfu' has been reported concerning this, but the apparent view is that it is not sound. Concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to the land which We have blessed﴾, there are other opinions which we have left aside because of their weakness in our view.

In this noble verse there is evidence that fleeing with one's religion from the abode of disbelief to a land where the one fleeing can establish his religion is obligatory. This type of migration remains obligatory, with no disagreement among the scholars regarding this.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 72:**

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift (nafilah), and We made each of them righteous.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that He granted Abraham his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, and that He made all of them righteous. He has clarified the glad tidings of both of them in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed. Then We gave her good tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71], and His saying: ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat: 112]. In Surah Maryam, Allah, Exalted, also indicated that when Abraham left his homeland and his relatives, Allah compensated him for that with comfort to the eye through righteous offspring. That is in His saying: ﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We made each of them a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 49].

As for His saying in this noble verse, "nafilah" (additional gift), Ibn Kathir said about it: Ata and Mujahid said: "nafilah" means "a gift." Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Hakam ibn Utaybah said: "an-nafilah" is the son's son, meaning that Jacob was the son of Isaac.

Its annotator, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The root meaning of "nafilah" in the language is an increase over the original. From it comes "an-nawafil" in acts of worship, because they are increases over the original, which is the obligation. A grandson is an increase over the original, which is the son of the loins. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*If she is a noble female from Ma'add, who is above us, then you have given her an additional excellence (nafilat al-fadl).*

That is, you have given her superiority over us, and an increase in honor over us. This is the correct meaning of Abu Dhu'ayb's verse, as Abu Sa'id al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn as-Sukkari explained it in his commentary on the poetry of the Hudhaylites. From this you know that the author of Lisan al-Arab's citation of Abu Dhu'ayb's verse as evidence that "an-nafilah" means "booty" is not correct; rather, it is an error. Moreover, al-anfal, which are the spoils of war, return in meaning to the sense of increase, because they are an increase of honor with which Allah honored this noble Prophet, so He made them lawful for him and for his community. Or because the captured wealth is wealth they took as an increase over their original wealth without price.

His saying "nafilah" has two possible grammatical analyses (i'rab). According to the one who said that "an-nafilah" means "a gift," it is what stands in for the absolute object (al-mutlaq) of "wahabna," meaning: We gave him Isaac and Jacob as a gift (hibah). On this view, "nafilah" is a verbal noun (masdar) that came in the form of the active participle, like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah. And according to the view that "an-nafilah" means "an increase," it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "Ya'qub," meaning: We gave him Jacob in the state of being an increase over Isaac.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 73:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah. And they were worshippers of Us.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "We made them" (jaʿalnāhum) includes all those previously mentioned: Ibrahim, Lut, Ishaq, and Yaʿqub, as Abu Hayyan affirmed in *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, and this is the apparent meaning.

This noble verse indicates that Allah made Ishaq and Yaʿqub among the leaders (a-aʾimmah), meaning He made them leaders in religion, who are followed in good deeds and acts of obedience. His saying "by Our command" means: by what We sent down to them of revelation, command, and prohibition. Or it means they guide people to Our religion by Our command to them, by guiding creation and calling them to monotheism.

This noble verse also clarifies that Ibrahim's request for leadership for his descendants, mentioned in *al-Baqarah*, was answered with regard to some of his descendants but not others. The governing principle is that the wrongdoers among his descendants do not attain leadership, unlike others such as Ishaq and Yaʿqub, who do attain it, as Allah stated explicitly in His saying here: ﴿And We made them leaders﴾ [21] (p-167). Ibrahim's request is what is mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tried by his Lord with commands, and he fulfilled them, He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." [Ibrahim] said, "And of my descendants?" [Allah] said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. So His saying "And of my descendants" means: appoint from my descendants leaders who are followed in goodness. Allah answered him with His saying: "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers," meaning: My covenant of leadership does not reach the wrongdoers, according to the more correct view. The implication of His saying "the wrongdoers" is that others do attain His covenant of leadership, as He stated explicitly here. This distinction mentioned regarding the descendants of Ibrahim was indicated by Allah, may He be exalted, in *al-Saffat* by His saying: ﴿And among their descendants are one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾ [al-Saffat: 113]

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And We revealed to them the doing of good deeds﴾ [21] means: that they should perform acts of obedience and command people to perform them. The establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah are among the good deeds, so this is an instance of ʿatf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm (the conjunction of the specific over the general). I have previously mentioned several times the rhetorical point that justifies iṭnāb (elaboration) in conjoining the specific over the general, and its reverse in the Qur'an, so that suffices here and there is no need to repeat it.

His saying "and they were worshippers of Us" means: obedient to Us by refraining from what is forbidden and carrying out commands sincerely. They do what they command people to do and avoid what they forbid them from, as the prophet of Allah Shuʿayb said: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in that which I forbid you from.﴾ [Hud: 88]

His saying "a-aʾimmah" (leaders) is known to be the plural of imam, and the imam is the one who is followed. The term is used for good, as here, and for evil, as in His saying: ﴿And We made them leaders who call to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas: 41]. What al-Zamakhshari supposed to be a difficulty in this verse is not actually a difficulty, as Abu Hayyan pointed out. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: "iqama al-salah" (إقامَ الصَّلاةِ) did not have a taʾ (ة) compensate for the dropped ʿayn here, due to the well-known morphological rule of iʿlal (morphological weakening). This is because omitting the compensation is permissible, as is the case here, as indicated in the *Khulasa* by its statement:

"... and the alif of al-ifʿal and istifʿal ..."

"Remove it for the sake of iʿlal, and make the taʾ obligatory as compensation; its omission by transposition may occasionally occur."

He also indicated in the chapter on the patterns of verbal nouns (masdar) that the compensatory taʾ for the ʿayn is the more common, by his statement:

"Seek refuge with ʾistiʿadhah, then establish iqamah; and generally the one with taʾ is obligatory."

What he mentioned, that the taʾ mentioned is a compensation for the ʿayn, is better than the view of those who said that the ʿayn remains, being the remaining alif, and that the taʾ is a compensation for the alif of al-ifʿal (p-168).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 74:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We delivered him from the town that was committing abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was among the righteous.﴾

His statement: "Lūtan" (Lot) [21] is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted obligatorily, which is explained by "ātaynāhu" (We gave him), as he said in the Khulasa (the poetic summary of grammar by Ibn Malik):

"The preceding noun is put in the accusative by a verb that is necessarily omitted, one that agrees with what has been made apparent."

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse: "Al-ḥukm" (judgment) is prophethood. "Al-ʿilm" (knowledge) is knowledge of the matters of religion and that by which judgment is made between disputants. It has been said: "ʿIlman" means understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ḥukman" means wisdom, which is what ought to be done, or a decisive judgment between disputants. It has also been said that it is prophethood.

His commentator, may Allah pardon him, said: The original meaning of "ḥukm" in the language is prevention, as is well known. So the meaning of the verses is that Allah gave him, of prophethood and knowledge, what prevents his words and deeds from being touched by flaw. The town that was committing abominations is Sodom and its practices. The abominations it committed have come clarified in verses of the Book of Allah:

Among them: sodomy (liwāṭ), and that they were the first of mankind to do it, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do you commit an indecency that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80] and He said: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds and leave what your Lord has created for you of your wives? Rather, you are a people transgressing.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 165–166]. Among the abominations mentioned is their committing the evil in their gatherings and their highway robbery, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do you indeed approach men and cut off the way and commit evil in your gatherings?﴾ the verse [al-'Ankabut: 29]. Among the greatest of their abominations: their denial of the Prophet of Allah, Lot, and their threat to him of expulsion from the homeland, as Allah, the Exalted, said of them: ﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be among the expelled."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 167] and Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and other verses. Allah has made clear in several places in His Book that He destroyed them, overturning their land and raining upon them stones of baked clay (sijjil), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of hard clay﴾ [15]. The verses to this effect are many. "Al-khabā'ith" (the abominations) is the plural of "khabītha," which is the evil act, such as disbelief, sodomy, and what is similar to them.

(p-169) As for His statement "qawma saw'" (a people of evil), meaning: possessors of evil deeds, and for them with Allah is a recompense that will distress them. As for His statement "fāsiqīn" (defiantly disobedient), meaning: going out of obedience to Allah. As for His statement "wa-adkhalnāhu" (And We admitted him), meaning Lot, "fī raḥmatinā" (into Our mercy), it includes his deliverance from their punishment that befell them, and it includes his admission into His mercy, which is Paradise, as in the authentic hadith: "The Fire and the Garden disputed..." — the hadith. And in it: "He said to the Garden: 'You are My mercy; through you I show mercy to whomever I will of My servants.'"

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 76:

Allah's saying: ﴿And Noah, when he called out before; so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾ ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all.﴾

His saying: "Nuhan" (And Noah) is in the accusative, governed by an implied "udhkur" (mention/remember), meaning: and mention Noah when he called out before, that is, before Ibrahim and those mentioned with him. The calling of Noah mentioned here is the one referred to in Allah's saying: ﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us, and We are the best of responders﴾ ﴿And We delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾ ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat: 75–77]. Allah has clarified this calling in His saying: ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant"﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except wicked disbelievers﴾ [Nuh: 26–27], and His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them; they denied Our servant and said, "Mad!" and he was rebuked﴾ ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overpowered, so give victory"﴾ ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring forth﴾ [al-Qamar: 9–11].

The "great distress" in the verse means drowning by the flood, whose waves surge like great mountains, as Allah says: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains﴾ [Hud: 42], and He says: ﴿But We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾ [al-Ankabut: 15], and other verses. "Al-karb" (distress) is the utmost grief and the seizing of the soul.

As for Allah's saying in this noble verse, "fanajjaynahu wa-ahlahu" (so We delivered him and his family), it means except those among his family against whom the word had already gone forth for destruction along with the disbelieving destroyed ones, as Allah says: ﴿We said, "Load therein of each kind two, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth"﴾ [Hud: 40]. Among those against whom the word had gone forth were his son, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And a wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud: 43], and his wife, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿"Enter the Fire with those who enter."﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10].

[p. 170]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the tilth, when the sheep of certain people grazed in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. So We gave understanding of it to Solomon; and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: "David" [al-Anbiya′: 78] is in the accusative, governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur). It has also been said that it is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And Noah, when he called out before [that]﴾ [21], meaning: "And remember Noah when he called out before, and David and Solomon when they gave judgment concerning the tilth," and so on through the verse.

His saying "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "David and Solomon," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), as we made clear in the surah of Maryam, where we also mentioned some discussion of it. We have already stated, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the kinds of clarification (bayan) it contains is that some scholars state an opinion about a verse while there is within the same verse an indication (qarinah) that points against that opinion. We have mentioned many issues of this kind in this book. Knowing this, be aware that a group of scholars said: the judgment of David and Solomon concerning the tilth mentioned in this verse was by revelation (wahy), except that what was revealed to Solomon abrogated (nasikh) what was revealed to David.

But the verse contains two indications that their judgment was by independent reasoning (ijtihad) and not by revelation, and that Solomon was correct and merited praise for his ijtihad and his correctness, while David was not correct and merited praise for his ijtihad, and did not deserve blame or reproach for his incorrectness. He praised Solomon for correctness in His saying: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 79], and He praised both of them in His saying: ﴿and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 78]. His saying "when they gave judgment" indicates that both of them judged in it together, each one giving a judgment different from the other's; and had it been revelation, the difference would not have been permissible. Then He said: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, which indicates that David did not understand it. Had his judgment in it been by revelation, he would have been given understanding of it, as you see. So His saying "when they gave judgment" together with His saying "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" is an indication that the judgment was not by revelation but by ijtihad, and that Solomon was correct in it rather than David, by God's granting him that understanding.

The second indication is that His saying, may He be exalted, "So We gave understanding of it" indicates that He gave him understanding of it from the texts of the law (shar′) that they had. It does not mean that He sent down to him a new, abrogating revelation concerning it; for His saying "So We gave understanding of it" is more fitting to the first case than to the second, as you see.

* * *

Issues related to this noble verse

First issue:

Know that what we have mentioned, that the indication points in this verse to their judgment being by ijtihad, and that Solomon was correct in his ijtihad, has been confirmed by authentic Sunnah with the occurrence of the like of it from them in a case other than this. This indicates its possibility in this case, and the Qur'anic indication has pointed to its occurrence. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih (Chapter: When a woman claims a son): Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Shu′ayb informed us, Abu al-Zinad narrated to us, from al-A′raj, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two women were with their two sons. A wolf came and took away the son of one of them. She said to her companion: 'It was your son that the wolf took.' The other said: 'It was your son that it took.' So they brought their dispute to David, peace be upon him, and he judged for the elder. Then they went out to Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both, and informed him, and he said: 'Bring me a knife, and I will cut him between you.' The younger said: 'Do not do that, may Allah have mercy on you; he is her son.' So he judged for the younger." Abu Hurayrah said: "By Allah, I had never heard of a knife (sikkin) except on that day, and we used to say only al-mudyah." End of quotation from Sahih al-Bukhari.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj said in his Sahih: Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to me, Shababah narrated to me, Warqa′ narrated to me, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-A′raj, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While two women were with their two sons, a wolf came and took away the son of one of them. This one said to her companion: 'It was only your son that it took.' The other said: 'It was only your son that it took.' So they brought their dispute to David, and he judged for the elder. Then they went out to Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both, and informed him, and he said: 'Bring me a knife, and I will cut him between you.' The younger said: 'No, may Allah have mercy on you.'" End of quotation from it.

This sound hadith clearly indicates that the two of them judged together by ijtihad concerning the son mentioned, and that Solomon was correct in that. For had David's judgment been by revelation, it would never have been permissible to overturn it. And it is clear that Solomon's judgment was not by revelation, because he gave the two women the impression that he would cut the child with the knife, so that he might know the mother by her compassion for him, and know the liar by her consent to his being cut, so that the true mother would share her loss with her; and thus he recognized the truth. This is very similar to what the verse indicates, as we have stated and explained the indication of the Qur'anic qarinah for it.

Similar to these two judgments is the story that the hafiz Abu al-Qasim ibn ′Asakir related in the biography of Solomon, peace be upon him, in his History (Tarikh), through the chain of al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, from Safwan ibn Salih, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, and from Sa′id ibn Bishr, from Qatadah, from Mujahid, from Ibn ′Abbas. He related a lengthy story, the summary of which is that a beautiful woman in the time of the Children of Israel was solicited by four of their leaders, but she refused each of them. They agreed among themselves against her. They testified before David, peace be upon him, that she had given herself to a dog of hers which she had trained to do that, so he ordered her stoning. When it was evening that day, Solomon sat, and boys like him gathered with him. He stood up as a judge, and four of them dressed in the garb of those men, and another dressed in the garb of the woman. They testified against her that she had given herself to a dog. Solomon said: "Separate them." He asked the first: "What was the color of the dog?" He said: "Black," so he dismissed him. He summoned the next and asked him about its color. He said: "Red." The next said: "Dusky." The next said: "White." So at that he ordered them executed. This was reported to David, peace be upon him, and he immediately summoned those four and asked them separately about the color of that dog, and they disagreed, so he ordered them executed. End of quotation through the transmission of Ibn Kathir in his commentary on this noble verse. All of this indicates the correctness of what we have interpreted the verse to mean, because of the indication of the Qur'anic qarinah for it.

Among those who interpreted it this way is al-Hasan al-Basri, as al-Bukhari and others mention from him. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih, under the chapter "When a man deserves to judge": Al-Hasan said: Allah took a covenant from the judges that they should not follow their desires, nor fear people, "and do not exchange My signs for a small price" [al-Baqarah: 41]. Then he said, and he recited: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the tilth...﴾ to ﴿...and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 78–79]. So he praised Solomon and did not blame David. Had it not been for what Allah mentioned about these two, I would have thought that the judges were lost, for He praised this one for his knowledge and excused that one for his ijtihad. End of the relevant point of his quotation.

From this you know that al-Hasan holds that the meaning of the noble verse is as we have mentioned. And what further clarifies this is what we have already presented in the surah of Bani Isra′il, from the hadith agreed upon (muttafaq ′alayh) from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the hadiths of ′Amr ibn al-′As and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When a judge judges and exerts himself (ijtahada) and is correct, he has two rewards; and when he judges and exerts himself and is mistaken, he has one reward," as we have already explained.

* * *

Second issue:

Know that ijtihad in the rulings of the law is indicated by evidences from the Book and the Sunnah, of which this that we have mentioned here is one. We already presented a part of this in the surah of Bani Isra′il, and promised to mention it fully in this surah and in surah al-Hashr. This is the time to fulfill that promise in this noble surah. You have learned from what passed in the surah of Bani Isra′il that we mentioned a portion of the evidences for ijtihad, and we demonstrated the consensus of the scholars on acting by the type of ijtihad known as ilhaq bi-nafy al-fariq (extension by negating any difference), which al-Shafi′i calls qiyas fi ma′na al-asl (analogy in the meaning of the source), and which is tanqih al-manat (purifying the ratio legis). We clarified that no one denies it except an obstinate person. We also demonstrated the consensus on acting by the type of ijtihad known as tahqiq al-manat (verifying the ratio legis in the case), and that no one denies it except an obstinate person. We mentioned examples of it from the Book and the Sunnah, and we mentioned hadiths indicating ijtihad, among them the agreed-upon hadith already cited, and among them the hadith of Mu′adh when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen. We promised to mention its chains here, up to the end of what we mentioned there.

[p. 173] Know that all the transmissions of this hadith mentioned in the Musnad and the Sunan come through the chain of Shu′bah, from Abu ′Awn, from al-Harith ibn ′Amr, the nephew of al-Mughirah ibn Shu′bah, from some people among the companions of Mu′adh, from Mu′adh, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for the connected, sound transmission that we mentioned earlier from Ibn Qudamah in (Rawdat al-Nazir), that ′Ubadah ibn Nusayy narrated it from ′Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Mu′adh: this chain, though connected and its narrators known for reliability, I have not found anyone who transmitted this hadith by this route except what the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in (I′lam al-Muwaqqi′in) from Abu Bakr al-Khatib, with the wording: "It has been said that ′Ubadah ibn Nusayy narrated it from ′Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Mu′adh." End of quotation from it. The expression "it has been said" (qila) is a form of weakening (tamrid), as is well known. Apart from that, there is what Ibn Kathir mentioned in his History, for when he related this hadith of Mu′adh in the wording we mentioned, with the chain by which Imam Ahmad transmitted it, he said: Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it from the hadith of Shu′bah with it. al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know it except through this route, and its chain, in my view, is not connected." Then Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Majah also transmitted it from another route, from him, but by way of Muhammad ibn Sa′id ibn Hassan, who was crucified and was one of the liars, from ′Ubadah ibn Nusayy, from ′Abd al-Rahman, from Mu′adh, with something similar.

Know that the copy of Ibn Kathir's History in our hands, which is of the first edition of the year (1351), contains a typographical error in the passage we quoted: it has "Muhammad ibn Sa′d ibn Hassan," whereas the correct reading is "Muhammad ibn Sa′id," not "Sa′d." And it has "from ′Iyadh ibn Bishr," whereas the correct reading is "from ′Ubadah ibn Nusayy."

Ibn Kathir's citation of Ibn Majah's transmission of the hadith of Mu'adh, through the route of Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Maslub, from Ubadah ibn Nusayy, from Abd al-Rahman, namely Ibn Ghanm, from Mu'adh, I have not found in the Sunan of Ibn Majah. What is in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, with the stated isnad, from the hadith of Mu'adh, is other than the stated text, and this is its wording: "Al-Hasan ibn Hammad Sajjadah narrated to us, Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Umawi narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn Hassan, from Ubadah ibn Nusayy, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, 'Mu'adh ibn Jabal narrated to us, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to Yemen, and said: "Do not judge, nor decide [any matter], except by what you know. If a matter becomes unclear to you, then pause until you clarify it, or write to me concerning it."'" End of his quotation. I do not know whether al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir erred in what he mentioned, or whether he believes that the meaning of "tabayyanahu" in the hadith is: you know it through your ijtihad in deriving it from the explicit texts, so that it returns to the meaning of the aforementioned hadith? In any case, the aforementioned narration through the route of Ubadah ibn Nusayy, from Ibn Ghanm, from Mu'adh, contains a liar, namely Muhammad ibn Sa'id mentioned above, whom Abu Ja'far al-Mansur killed for zandaqah (heresy) and crucified. Ahmad ibn Salih said: he fabricated four thousand hadiths. Having learned this, you know the reason for the weakening of the hadith by those who weakened it, the hadith in which Mu'adh said to the Prophet (ﷺ) that if he did not find the matter in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would exercise his own opinion (ijtihad) concerning it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved of that in the two aforementioned routes. They say: the route of Ubadah ibn Nusayy from Ibn Ghanm has not been established by us as reliable through a sound channel to him, and the other route found in the Musnad and the Sunan contains al-Harith ibn Akhi al-Mughirah, who is unknown (majhul), and the narrators in it from Mu'adh are also unknown. So from where do you say it is authentic? We have already mentioned that Ibn Kathir said in the introduction to his tafsir: the route mentioned in the Musnad and the Sunan is with a good isnad. We said: perhaps he regards al-Harith mentioned as trustworthy (thiqah), and Ibn Hibban has declared him trustworthy, and that none of Mu'adh's companions is known to be a liar or accused.

The one who wrote these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What supports what we have mentioned about Ibn Kathir's intention regarding the goodness of the aforementioned isnad is what the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in. He said therein: The Prophet (ﷺ) approved of Mu'adh's exercise of his opinion in matters on which he found no explicit text from Allah and His Messenger. Shu'bah said: Abu Awn narrated to me from al-Harith ibn Amr, "from some people among the companions of Mu'adh: that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, he said: 'How will you act if a judgment comes before you?' He said: I will judge by what is in the Book of Allah. He said: 'And if it is not in the Book of Allah?' He said: Then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'And if it is not in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' He said: I will exercise my own opinion, and I will not fall short. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck my chest and then said: 'Praise be to Allah who has granted success to the messenger of the Messenger of Allah with what pleases the Messenger of Allah.'" This is a hadith which, even if it is narrated from unnamed people, they are the companions of Mu'adh, and that does not harm it, because it indicates the fame of the hadith, and that al-Harith ibn Amr narrated it from a group of Mu'adh's companions, not from one of them alone, and this is more emphatic in fame than if it were from one of them, even if named. How could it not be so, when the fame of Mu'adh's companions for knowledge, religion, virtue and truthfulness is at a level that is not hidden, and no one among his companions is known as accused, a liar, or discredited; rather his companions are among the most excellent and best of the Muslims, and the people of knowledge of transmission have no doubt about that. How could it be otherwise when Shu'bah is the bearer of the banner of this hadith? Some of the imams of hadith said: when you see Shu'bah in the isnad of a hadith, grip it with both your hands. Abu Bakr al-Khatib said: It has been said that Ubadah ibn Nusayy narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Mu'adh, and this is a connected isnad, and its narrators are known for reliability, and the people of knowledge have transmitted it and relied upon it. Thereby we know its authenticity according to them, just as we know by the same means the authenticity of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no bequest to an heir"; and his saying concerning the sea: "Its water is pure, and its dead animals are lawful"; and his saying: "If the two sellers disagree about the price while the goods are still present, they shall swear and the sale shall be annulled"; and his saying: "The blood money is upon the paternal kin ('aqilah)." Even though these hadiths are not established in terms of isnad, yet because the whole community received them from the whole community, they were independent of seeking an isnad for them. Likewise the hadith of Mu'adh: since they all relied upon it, they were independent of seeking an isnad for it. End of his quotation. The hadith of Amr ibn al-As and Abu Hurayrah, which is established in the two Sahihs, is a witness to it, as we mentioned, and it has other witnesses besides that, which you will see, Allah willing.
