The third issue:

Know that ijtihad, as indicated by the texts of the Shari'ah, has several types:

(Among them): ijtihad in tahqiq al-manat (verifying the effective cause in a particular case), of which we have already mentioned many examples in "al-Isra'".

(Among them): ijtihad in tanqih al-manat (purifying the effective cause from extraneous features), and among its kinds are: sabr (examining the possible causes), taqsim (division), and al-ilhaq bi-nafy al-fariq (attaching by negating the difference).

Know that ijtihad by attaching the unmentioned to the mentioned is of two kinds:

The first: al-ilhaq bi-nafy al-fariq (attaching by negating the difference), which is a type of tanqih al-manat as we mentioned just now. It is called by al-Shafi'i qiyas fi ma'na al-asl (analogy in the meaning of the original), and it is exactly the same as mafhum al-muwafaqah (implicit agreement of meaning), and it is also called qiyas al-jali (the clear analogy).

The second of the two types of attachment is what is known by this name in the terminology of the jurists of usul: qiyas (analogy).

As for the first type, which is attaching by negating the difference, it does not require a common descriptive attribute (wasf jami') between the original and the derivative, which is the 'illah (effective cause). Rather it is said of it: there is found between this mentioned matter and this unmentioned matter no difference that affects the ruling at all, so it is like it in the ruling. Its divisions are four, because the unmentioned matter is either equal to the mentioned matter in the ruling, or more deserving of it than it; and in each of these two cases the negation of difference between them is either certain or probable. Thus the total is four:

(The first of them): that the unmentioned matter is more deserving of the ruling than the mentioned matter, with certainty of negating the difference, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. The unmentioned act of striking is more deserving of the ruling, which is prohibition, than the mentioned uff, with certainty of negating the difference. And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. The testimony of four just men, which is not mentioned, is more deserving of the ruling, which is acceptance, than the mentioned testimony of two just men, with certainty of negating the difference.

(The second of them): that the unmentioned matter is also more deserving of the ruling than the mentioned matter, but the negation of difference between them is not certain, rather probable with a strong assumption close to certainty. Its example is his prohibition (ﷺ) of sacrificing a one-eyed animal (al-'awra'). The sacrifice of a blind animal, which is unmentioned, is more deserving of the ruling, which is the prohibition of sacrifice, than the mentioned one-eyed animal, but the negation of difference between them is not certain, rather probable with a strong assumption; because the 'illah of the prohibition of sacrificing the one-eyed animal is that it is defective in its body, its price and its value, and this is the apparent meaning, and on this basis the blind animal is more defective than it in body and value. There is another possibility, which is what prevented certainty about negating the difference, namely the possibility that the 'illah of the prohibition of sacrificing the one-eyed animal is that blindness is a likely cause of emaciation, because the one-eyed animal has defective sight, and defective sight means defective grazing, since it sees only what faces one eye, and defective grazing is a likely cause of emaciation. On this aspect, the blind animal is not like the one-eyed, because the blind animal is given the best fodder, so this becomes a likely cause of its fatness.

(The third of them): that the unmentioned matter is equal to the mentioned matter in the ruling with certainty of negating the difference; like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa': 10] etc. The burning and drowning of the property of orphans, which is unmentioned, is equal to the mentioned devouring in the ruling, which is prohibition and the threat of the punishment of the Fire, with certainty of negating the difference.

(The fourth of them): that the unmentioned matter is also equal to the mentioned matter in the ruling, but the negation of difference between them is assumed with a strong assumption close to certainty. Its example is the sound hadith: "Whoever frees his share in a slave..." mentioned earlier in "al-Isra' and al-Kahf". The unmentioned matter, which is the freeing of part of a female slave, is equal to the mentioned matter, which is the freeing of part of a male slave, in the ruling, which is the spread of manumission (sirayah al-'itq), explained in the hadith mentioned earlier many times. However, the negation of difference between them is assumed with a strong assumption, because maleness and femaleness with respect to manumission are accompanying attributes (tardiyyan) on which no ruling of the rulings of manumission is based, as we have already mentioned fully in Surat Maryam. There is another possibility which prevented certainty of negating the difference, namely the possibility that the Lawgiver specified the spread of manumission in particular for the male slave, restricting that ruling to him and not the female; because the freeing of a male has legal consequences that do not follow from freeing a female, such as jihad, leadership, judgeship, and similar offices restricted to males and not females. We have given many examples of this type, which is attachment by negating the difference, in Surat Bani Isra'il.

(As for the second type of attachment): it is qiyas known in the usul, which is known as qiyas al-tamthil (analogy by similitude). We will define it here linguistically and technically, mention its divisions, and what some scholars have mentioned of its examples in the Qur'an.

Know that qiyas linguistically means: measuring and equalizing. It is said: he measured the cloth with the cubit (dhira'), and he measured the wound with the probe (mil, with a kasra), which is the sounding instrument, when he determined its depth with it; for this reason the probe is called miqyas. From this meaning is the saying of al-Bu'ayth ibn Bishr describing a wound or a head-injury:

"When the skilled, expert physician measures it, its pus recedes, and its breaking-open (wahy) increases."

His saying "qasaha" means he determined its depth with the probe.

Al-Asi: the physician; al-Nitasi (with kasra or fatha on the nun): the one skilled in medicine; al-Ghathithah (with two thas): the discharge of the wound and its pus, and the dead flesh in it; al-Wahy: tearing and splitting; al-Huzum: pressing a thing with the hand so that a hollow forms in it, as happens in severe swelling.

As for the definition of qiyas in the terminology of the jurists of usul, the expressions of the usuliyyun have multiplied concerning it, with well-known debates over their definitions. A number of them chose to define it as: carrying a known matter upon a known matter, that is, attaching it to it in its ruling because of equality with it in the effective cause of the ruling. This definition covers only sound qiyas and not invalid qiyas. The definition that covers the invalid is to add to the definition of the sound the phrase "according to the one who carries it" (inda al-hamil), so you say: it is the attaching of a known matter in its ruling to another because of equality with it in the effective cause of the ruling according to the one who carries it, so the invalid enters the definition along with the sound, as the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud indicated in defining qiyas:

"A known matter is carried upon what is already known, for equality in the effective cause of the ruling; and name it so."
"If you intend its inclusion of what is invalid, add 'according to the one who carries it,' and Zayd is a lion (asad)."

It is known that the pillars of the aforementioned qiyas are four: the original which is compared to (al-asl al-maqis 'alayhi), the derivative which is compared (al-far' al-maqis), the common effective cause between them ('illah jami'ah), and the ruling of the original which is compared to.

If we were to compare nabidh (date wine) to khamr (wine), then the original is khamr, the derivative is nabidh, the effective cause is intoxication (iskar), and the ruling of the original, which is khamr, is prohibition. The conditions of these four pillars and the discussion of them are fully treated in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), so we will not lengthen the discussion of them here.

Know that the aforementioned analogy (qiyas) is divided, in terms of the element that links the subsidiary case (far') and the original case (asl), into three types:

The first: qiyas al-'illa (analogy based on the effective cause).
The second: qiyas al-dalala (analogy based on indication).
The third: qiyas al-shabah (analogy based on resemblance).

As for qiyas al-'illa, its defining feature is that the linking between the subsidiary and the original case is by the very 'illa (effective cause) of the ruling. Thus the linking of nabidh (date or grape infusion) with khamr (wine) by the very 'illa, which is intoxication (iskar), is of this type. The intention here is simply illustration, because we have already established that analogy of nabidh upon khamr is not valid, given the text stating that every intoxicant is khamr, and that whatever in large quantity intoxicates, its small quantity is also forbidden. Analogy is not valid where the text explicitly states that the ruling of the subsidiary case is the same as the ruling of the original case. However, the example is valid by way of assumption, supposition, and mere possibility, as has already been mentioned. Similarly, the linking of wheat (bur) with maize (dhurra) by the very 'illa, which is measurement by volume (kayl), for example, according to those who hold this view. To this Ibn Malik's... [see below] the author of Maraqi (al-Su'ud) alluded in his verse:

*"What has been linked by the very 'illa, in it,
Is qiyas al-'illa, which has been heard of."*

As for qiyas al-dalala, its defining feature is that the linking in it is by means of an indicator of the 'illa, not by the 'illa itself. For example, one links the subsidiary and original cases by a necessary concomitant of the 'illa, or by its effect, or by its ruling. An example of linking by a necessary concomitant of the 'illa is: "Nabidh is forbidden like khamr, by the common attribute of intoxicating strength (al-shiddah al-mutribah), which is a necessary concomitant of intoxication, in the sense that its existence necessarily entails the existence of intoxication."

An example of linking by the effect of the 'illa is: "Killing by a blunt instrument requires retaliation (qisas), like killing by a sharp instrument, by the common attribute of sin (ithm), which is the effect of the 'illa, and the 'illa is deliberate, aggressive killing."

An example of linking by the ruling of the 'illa is: "A group is to be executed for one person's killing, just as they are killed for him, by the common attribute of the obligation of blood-money (diyah) upon them in that case, where the act was not deliberate. This is the ruling of the 'illa, which in the first example is the cutting (qat') done by them, and in the second is their killing."

To the definition of the aforementioned qiyas al-dalala the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud alluded in his verse:

*"The common element of the one with indication, which is necessarily connected,
Has an effect, and its ruling is as it is laid down."*

His words "alladhi lazima" (which is necessarily connected), in the active form, mean "the necessary concomitant" (al-lazim). His expressing it here as "al-lazim", following others, is an error on his part and on the part of those who followed him. This is because the existence of the necessary concomitant does not constitute evidence for the existence of the necessitating element (al-malzum), by the consensus of rational people, since it is possible that the necessary concomitant is more general than the necessitating element, and the existence of the more general does not entail the existence of the more specific, as is well known. For this reason, the scholars of theory (al-nuzzar) unanimously agreed that affirming the consequent in a connected conditional does not yield affirming the antecedent, because the existence of the necessary concomitant does not entail the existence of the necessitating element. The correct view is what we have illustrated with the linking by the necessitating element of the 'illa, because the necessitating element is that whose existence entails the existence of the necessary concomitant, as is well known. Thus intoxicating strength and intoxication are mutually implicative, and the indication of intoxicating strength upon intoxication is only in that it is a necessitating element of it, not a necessary concomitant, for you know that the existence of the necessary concomitant does not entail the existence of the necessitating element. Its entailing it here is only due to the mutual implication between the two extremes, since each of them is a necessary concomitant of the other and a necessitating element of it, due to the mutual implication between them from both sides.

As for qiyas al-shabah, the expressions of the scholars of legal theory (usul) have differed concerning it. Some of them defined shabah as "a position between the relevant attribute (munasib) and the arbitrary attribute (tard)," and some defined it as "the relevant attribute by way of consequence, not in itself." The meaning of this is like the meaning of the definition of one who defined it as "that which necessitates the relevant attribute."

The author of these notes, may God pardon him and forgive him, says: The expressions of the scholars of legal theory regarding shabah, which is the sixth of the methods of establishing the 'illa according to the Malikis and Shafi'is, all revolve around one thing, which is that the descriptive attribute that links in shabah-analogy resembles the relevant attribute in one respect, and resembles the arbitrary attribute in another respect.

We have already mentioned in the chapter of Maryam that the relevant attribute (munasib) is that attribute whose association of the ruling with it contains a benefit, either in bringing about a gain or in averting a harm, while the arbitrary attribute (tardi) is that which is not so, either in all rulings or in some of them. There is no disagreement among the scholars of legal theory that what is called "predominance of resemblances" (ghalabat al-ashbah) does not fall outside qiyas al-shabah. Some of them say it is included within it, and this is the apparent view; and some say it is precisely that and nothing else. The predominance of resemblances is the attachment of a subsidiary case that is ambiguous between two original cases to the one it more closely resembles. For example, a slave: he is ambiguous between two original cases because he resembles each of them. He resembles property, because he is sold, bought, gifted, and inherited, and other conditions of property; and he resembles the free person, in that he is a human being who marries, divorces, is rewarded and punished, and is bound by the commands and prohibitions of the Law. Most scholars say that his resemblance to property is greater than his resemblance to the free person, because he resembles property in both ruling and attribute together more than he resembles the free person in both.

Among his resemblances to property in ruling: that he is sold, bought, and inherited, gifted and lent, given as dowry and in khul' (divorce by wife's request), pledged, and other financial dispositions.

Among his resemblances to property in attribute: that his value varies according to the variation of his attributes in quality and inferiority, like all other property. So if a person kills another's slave, he is obliged to pay his value, considering that his resemblance to property is predominant. Some scholars said: he is obliged to pay his blood-money (diyah) as for a free person, supposing that his resemblance to the free person is predominant. If it is said: by what means is this type, which is the predominance of resemblances, a type of shabah, since you have established that it is a position between the relevant and the arbitrary, so what is the basis of its being a position between the relevant and the arbitrary? The answer is that clarifying this is that his attributes that resemble property, such as that he is sold and bought, etc., are arbitrary in relation to the obligation of blood-money, because his being like property is not suitable to be the basis for the obligation of his blood-money if he is killed; and likewise his attributes that resemble the free person, such as that he is addressed, rewarded and punished, etc., are arbitrary in relation to the obligation of the value, because his being like a free person is not suitable to be the basis for the obligation of the value. Thus in this respect he resembles the arbitrary, as you see. As for the consequence of the value upon his attributes resembling the attributes of property, it is relevant, as you see; and likewise the consequence of blood-money upon his attributes resembling the attributes of the free person is relevant. By these two considerations, it becomes clear that it is a position between the relevant and the arbitrary.

Among examples of types of shabah other than the predominance of resemblances: the shabah in which the common attribute is not relevant in itself, but necessarily entails the relevant attribute in itself, and the Law has testified to the effect of its nearer genus upon the nearer genus of the ruling. For example, your saying about vinegar: "It is a liquid upon whose genus a bridge is not built; therefore it does not remove ritual impurity (hadath) nor the ruling of filth (khabath), by analogy with oil." Your saying "a bridge is not built upon its genus" is not relevant in itself, because building a bridge upon a liquid, in itself, is an arbitrary attribute; but it necessarily entails a relevant attribute, because the habitual practice is that a bridge is not built upon a small amount of liquid, but upon a large amount, like rivers; and smallness is relevant to the non-legislation, for purity in general, of liquids characterized by it, since the general Law requires that its causes be of general availability, whereas obligating everyone with what only some can find is far from the principles. So your saying "a bridge is not built upon its genus" has become not relevant, but it necessarily entails the relevant. The Law has testified to the effect of the genus of scarcity, and of the inability in the non-legislation of purification, by the evidence that when water is scarce and there is strong need for it, the command to purify with it falls, and one moves to tayammum (dry ablution).

As for the formal shabah (shabah suwari), we have already discussed it fully in the chapter of al-Nahl, in the discussion of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed in livestock there is a lesson for you; We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, from between digestive waste and blood, pure milk, palatable to drinkers.﴾ [al-Nahl: 66]. We have also mentioned, at the beginning of the chapter of Bara'ah, the words of Ibn al-'Arabi, in which he said: "Do you not see that Uthman and the eminent Companions, how they resorted to qiyas al-nisba (analogy by relation) when there was no explicit text, and saw that the story of Bara'ah resembles the story of al-Anfal, so they attached it to it? If analogy enters into the composition of the Qur'an, then what is your opinion about the other rulings?" To the aforementioned shabah the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud alluded in his verse:

*"The shabah that necessitates the relevant,
Like wudu' necessitates nearness (to God)."*

*"With the consideration of its nearer genus
In the like of the ruling, not the remote genus."*

*"Its suitability is not known except through the Law,
And no relevant attribute is attached to it by hearing."*

*"Wherever it is possible to analogize the 'illa,
Abandoning it is by consensus more established."*

*"Otherwise, in its acceptance there is hesitation;
The predominance of resemblances is the best of it."*

*"In the ruling and the attribute, then the ruling,
Then the attribute alone, according to the learned."*

*"And Ibn 'Uliyya saw for the formal (shabah) what
Analogy is for horses over donkeys."*

Know that qiyas al-tard (analogy of concomitance) applies to two matters, since "tard" is used in two senses. It is used for the arbitrary attribute that is not suitable for associating a ruling with it, because it is devoid of benefit, as when some who hold that wudu' is nullified by eating camel meat thought that the cause of nullification by it is heat, so he attached to it the meat of the gazelle, saying: "It nullifies wudu', by analogy with camel meat, by the common element of heat." This analogy is void, because the common attribute in it is arbitrary. Similar to it is every case in which the common attribute is arbitrary; and this is one of the two matters to which qiyas al-tard applies.

The second of the two is the analogy in which the common attribute is deduced by the eighth method known as "tard," which is the recurrent positive concomitance (al-dawran al-wujudi). Its clarification is that it is the co-occurrence of the ruling with the attribute in all its instances other than the instance in dispute, in existence only and not in non-existence. The disagreement about whether it indicates the 'illa is well known in the books of legal theory.

Know that analogy and what is connected to it are explained in the discipline of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). The indicators which show that a specific attribute is the 'illa of a specific ruling are the well-known "methods of establishing the 'illa" (masalik al-'illa). They number ten according to those who count among them ilgha' al-fariq (elimination of the distinguishing factor), and nine according to those who do not count it among them. They are: the explicit text (nass), consensus (ijma'), allusion (iyma'), sabr (systematic division and elimination), taqsim (division), munasaba (relevance), shabah (resemblance), dawaran (concomitance), tard (concomitant variation), tanqih al-manat (purification of the ground of the ruling), and ilgha' al-fariq. The verification is that it is a type of tanqih al-manat, as we have mentioned.

Some of them arranged them in the verse:

*"Arrange the methods of the 'illa: text, then consensus, then allusion, then sabr,
Relevance, likewise resemblance, then after it concomitance, and tard which continues,
Then purification of the ground, then eliminate the distinction,
And these are ten for one who wishes to limit them."*

The place of their clarification is the discipline of usul al-fiqh, and we have clarified them in other than this place.

As for the objections (qadh) to the evidence, whether analogy or otherwise, they are well known in the discipline of usul, and Shaykh 'Umar al-Fasi has briefly versified them, saying:

*"Objection by counter-example (naqd), and by breaking (kasr) together,
Failure of the reverse (takhalluf al-'aks), and by reversal (qalb), listen."*

*"Lack of effect (adam al-ta'thir) by the attribute, and in the root,
Then in the branch, then in the ruling, so follow."*

*"And refusal (man'), and distinction (farq), and by division (taqsim),
And by disagreement about the known governing principle (dabt)."*

*"And lack of precision (fuqdan al-indibat) and clarity (zuhur),
And scratching (khadsh) in the appropriateness (tanasub) of what has been mentioned."*

*"And that the ruling does not lead to
The intended purpose of the Law, the Mighty; so accept."*

*"And scratching in the positing (wad') and in the consideration (i'tibar),
And saying by the implication (qawl bil-muwjab), which carries weight."*

*"And begin with questioning (istifsar) regarding the generality (ijmal),
Or strangeness, without doubt."*

And it was not that we did not clarify here the methods (*masalik*) and the defects (*qawadih*) of analogy, because that would lead to tedious prolixity. Moreover, all of this is clarified in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*), and we have clarified it in other than this place. Our aim here is merely to draw attention to it in general terms, without detail.

Having known this, be aware that the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim, may Exalted Allah have mercy on him, quenched the thirst on these questions in a way that cannot be surpassed in his book *I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in 'an Rabb al-'Alamin* (*Informing the Signatories on behalf of the Lord of the Worlds*). Here, if Allah wills, we will mention comprehensive and beneficial sections of his words on this subject that we are concerned with. He said in his discussion of the words of the Commander of the Faithful, Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, in his famous letter to Abu Musa: "Then understanding, understanding in what is presented to you of what arises for you that is not in the Qur'an or the Sunnah. Then compare matters by analogy (*qiys*) at that time, know the similar cases, then pursue what you see to be the most beloved to Allah and the most resembling of the truth," his words being as follows:

This is one of the things on which the proponents of analogy (*al-qiyasiyyun*) rely in the Shari'ah. They say: "This is the letter of Umar to Abu Musa, and none of the Companions denied it. Rather, they were all in agreement on the validity of analogy, which is one of the principles of the Shari'ah, and no jurist can dispense with it." Allah, Exalted, has directed His servants to it in more than one place in His Book. He analogized the second creation to the first creation in terms of possibility, making the first creation the basis (*asl*) and the second a branch (*far'*) upon it. He analogized the life of the dead to the life of the earth after its death through vegetation. He analogized the new creation, which His enemies denied, to the creation of the heavens and the earth, and made it from the analogy of what is more fitting (*qiyas al-awla*), just as He made the analogy of the second creation to the first one from the analogy of what is more fitting. He analogized life after death to waking after sleep, and He coined parables and varied them in different kinds, and all of them are rational analogies by which He alerts His servants that the ruling on a thing is the ruling on its like, for all parables are analogies from which the ruling of the one represented is known from the one used as the representation. The Qur'an contains about forty-some parables that include the comparison of a thing with its counterpart and the equating of the two in ruling. Exalted is He said: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. The use of analogy in coining parables is among the special properties of reason. Allah has also embedded in the natures (*fitar*) and minds of people the equating of two alike things and the denial of distinguishing between them, and the distinguishing between two different things and the denial of joining them. They said: "The basis of inference (*istidlal*) is the aggregation (*jam'iyyah*) of equating like things and distinguishing unlike things. Inference is either: inference from a specific to a specific, or from a specific to a general, or from a general to a specific, or from a general to a general. These four are the comprehensive forms of inference. Inference from a specific to a specific is inference from the necessitating (*malzum*) to its necessary consequence (*lazim*), since every necessitating thing is evidence for its necessary consequence. If the necessitation is mutual, each of the two is evidence for the other and indicated by it. This type has three divisions: first, inference from the effective cause (*mu'aththir*) to the effect (*athar*); second, inference from the effect to the effective cause; third, inference from one of two effects to the other. The first is like inferring fire from burning. The second is like inferring burning from fire. The third is like inferring smoke from burning. All of this rests on necessitation. Equating two like things is inferring the establishment of one of the two effects from the other, while analogy of distinction is inferring the absence of one of the two effects from the absence of the other, or inferring the absence of the necessary consequence from the absence of its necessitating cause. So if it were permissible to distinguish between two like things, the path of inference would be blocked and its doors locked."

They said: "As for inference from a specific to a general, it is not complete except by equating like things, for if distinction were permissible, this specific would not be evidence for a general matter common to individuals. From this are the Qur'anic proofs of the punishment of specific people whom He punished for denying His messengers and disobeying His command, indicating that this ruling is general and encompasses whoever follows their path and has their attributes. He, glorified be He, has alerted His servants to this very method of inference, extending this particular to the general, as He said after informing about the punishments of the nations who denied their messengers and what befell them: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those, or do you have immunity in the scriptures?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43]. This is purely the extension of the ruling to others than those mentioned, by the generality of the cause (*'illah*). Otherwise, if the ruling on a thing were not the ruling on its like, the extension would not be binding and the proof would not be established. Similar to this is His saying, Exalted, after informing about the punishment of the people of Hud when they saw the cloud in the sky: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. He then said: ﴿Rather, it is what you were hastening for: a wind in which is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings. Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24-25]. Then He said: ﴿And We had established them in that wherein We have not established you, and We made for them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing and their sight and their hearts availed them nothing, since they used to deny the signs of Allah, and there encompassed them what they used to mock﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. Reflect on His saying: ﴿And We had established them in that wherein We have established you﴾, and you will find the meaning that your ruling is like their ruling, and that since We destroyed them for disobeying Our messenger, and what they were established in of the means of living did not repel it from them, you likewise are equal to them in that. The equating of two alike things is pure justice of Allah among His servants. Among this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled in the earth and looked at how the end of those before them was? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are the like of these﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. So He informed that the ruling on a thing is the ruling on its like. Likewise, every place where Allah, glorified be He, commanded travel in the earth, whether it is physical travel on foot or by beasts, or spiritual travel through reflection and contemplation, or whether the wording includes both, and this is the correct view, for it indicates taking heed and caution lest what befell those people befall the addressees. For this reason He, glorified be He, commanded those of insight to take heed of what befell the deniers. Had it not been that the ruling on the like is the ruling on its counterpart, such that minds pass from it to it, taking heed would not have been achieved. Allah, glorified be He, has negated from His judgment and wisdom the equating of those who differ in ruling. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals? What is wrong with you, how do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35-36], and informed that this judgment is false in natures and minds, and that attributing it to Him, glorified be He, is not fitting. Exalted He said: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21]. And Exalted He said: ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. Do you not see how He mentioned the minds and alerted the natures to what He placed in them of giving the counterpart the ruling of its counterpart, and of not equating a thing with its opposite in ruling? All of this is from the balance (*mizan*) that Allah sent down along with His Book, and made its companion and minister. Exalted He said: ﴿Allah is He who sent down the Book with truth and the balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. And He said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the balance so that people may establish justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. And Exalted He said: ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 1-2]. This is the Book. Then He said: ﴿And the heaven He raised and set up the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7]. The balance is intended to mean justice, and the instrument by which justice and its opposite are known. Correct analogy is the balance, so it is better to name it by the name Allah named it with, for it indicates justice, and it is a praiseworthy name, obligatory upon everyone at all times as far as possible. Unlike the name "qiyas," which is divided into true and false, and praiseworthy and blameworthy. For this reason, neither its praise nor its blame, nor the command to it, nor the prohibition of it, has come in the Qur'an, for it is subject to division into sound and unsound. The sound is the balance that Allah sent down with His Book, and the unsound is what opposes it, like the analogy of those who analogized sale to usury by the common feature of mutual exchange of property, and those who analogized carrion to slaughtered animals regarding the permissibility of eating them by the common feature of the taking of life, the one being by a human cause and the other by an act of Allah. For this reason you find in the words of the early generations (*salaf*) the censure of analogy and that it is not part of religion, and you also find in their words its use and reliance upon it. Both of these are true, as we shall explain, if Allah, Exalted, wills.

* *

The analogies used in inference are three: analogy of effective cause (*qiyas 'illah*), analogy of indication (*qiyas dalalah*), and analogy of resemblance (*qiyas shabah*), and all of them occur in the Qur'an. As for analogy of effective cause, it has come in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in several places. Among them is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. So He informed, Exalted, that Jesus is the counterpart of Adam in creation, by the common feature they share, which is the meaning on which the existence of all other creatures depends, namely their coming into being in obedience to His will and His creation. How, then, can one who admits the existence of Adam without father or mother, and the existence of Eve without a mother, deny the existence of Jesus without a father? Adam and Jesus are two counterparts, joined by that upon which the attribution of bringing into being and creation is valid.

Among them is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Already have passed before you examples; so travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137]. That is: There have been before you nations like you, so look at their evil ends, and know that the cause of that was their denial of the signs of Allah and His messengers. They are the basis (*asl*) and you are the branch (*far'*), the common cause (*'illah jami'ah*) is denial, and the ruling is destruction.

Among them is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established in the earth as We have not established you, and sent the sky upon them in abundance, and made rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins, and brought into being after them other generations﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. He, glorified be He, mentioned the destruction of the generations before us, and made clear that this occurred for the meaning of analogy, which is their sins. They are the basis and we are the branch, the sins are the common cause, and the ruling is destruction. This is purely analogy of effective cause, and He has confirmed it, glorified be He, by a form of what is more fitting, namely that those before us were stronger than us, yet their strength and might did not repel from them what befell them.

Among it is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Like those before you, who were more powerful than you and had more wealth and children, and they enjoyed their portion, and you have enjoyed your portion as those before you enjoyed their portion, and you plunged as they plunged. Those—their deeds are nullified in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69]. The position of this kaf (*"like"*) and what it relates to has been disputed. It is said: it is the nominative predicate of an omitted subject, i.e. "you are like those before you." It is said: it is in the accusative governed by an omitted verb, its estimate being: "you did as those before you did." The comparison, according to these two views, is in the deeds of those before. It is said: the comparison is in the punishment. Then it is said: the governing element is omitted, i.e. "He cursed and punished them as He cursed [those who were] before them." And it is said: rather the governing element is what precedes, i.e. "Allah's promise to the hypocrites is like the promise to those before you, and their curse is like their curse, and for them is a lasting punishment like the punishment that was theirs."

The intended meaning is that He, glory be to Him, joined them with those before them in the threat, and made them equal in it just as they were equal in their deeds. That they were stronger than the earlier people and had more wealth and children is a difference that has no effect. So He tied the ruling to the common, effective attribute and disregarded the distinguishing attribute. Then He drew attention to the fact that their sharing in the deeds required their sharing in the recompense, and said: ﴿So they enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share, and you have plunged as they plunged﴾ [9]. This is the effective cause ('illah mu'aththirah) and the common attribute (wasf jami'). His saying ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have failed﴾ is the ruling (hukm). Those before them are the original case (asl), and those addressed are the derived case (far').

'Abd al-Razzaq said in his Tafsir: Ma'mar related to us from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾, that he said: "with their religion." It is also reported from Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They enjoyed their portion of the Hereafter in this world." Others said: "with their portion of this world." The reality of the matter is that al-Khalaq (share, portion) means the allotted portion and lot, as though it is what was created for the human being and decreed for him, as one says: "his qasm (allotment) is that which was apportioned to him," and "his nasib (portion) is that which was set up for him," i.e., established; and "his qitt (lot) is that which was cut for him," i.e., severed. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he will have no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]. And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Only he who has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter wears silk in this world». The verse encompasses all that the Salaf mentioned, for He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾ [9]. By that power which they possessed, they were able to work for this world and the Hereafter. Likewise wealth and children; and that power, wealth and children are the khalaq. So they enjoyed their power and their wealth in this world, and the very deeds they performed with this power are part of the khalaq which they enjoyed.

Had they intended by that Allah and the Last Abode, they would have had a share in the Hereafter. Their enjoyment, then, is the taking of their hasty portions, and this is the condition of one who works only for his worldly life, whether his deed is of the kind of acts of worship or otherwise. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the derived case, saying: ﴿So you have enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share﴾. This indicates that their ruling is the same as their ruling, and that what befalls them will befall them, because the ruling for the like is the ruling for its like. Then He said: ﴿and you have plunged as they plunged﴾. It has been said that "alladhi" (as) is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "like the plunging of those who plunged." It has also been said that it is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: "like the plunging of the people who plunged," and it is the subject of the plunging (al-khawd).

It has also been said that "alladhi" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) like "ma," meaning: "like their plunging." And it has been said that it is in the position of "alladhina" (those who). The intended meaning is that He, glory be to Him, combined enjoying the khalaq with plunging into falsehood, because the corruption of religion either occurs through belief in falsehood and speaking it, which is plunging, or occurs through acting contrary to the truth, while the correct course is enjoying the khalaq. The first is innovation (bid'ah), and the second is following desire (ittiba' al-hawa). These two are the root of every evil, trial and affliction, and by them the Messengers were denied, the Lord was disobeyed, the Fire was entered, and punishments descended.

The first comes from the direction of doubts (shubuhat), and the second from the direction of desires (shahawat). For this reason the Salaf used to say: "Beware of two types of people: the possessor of desire, whom his desire has seduced, and the possessor of the world, whom his worldly life has impressed." And they used to say: "Beware of the trial of the wicked scholar and the ignorant worshipper, for their trial is a trial for every person who is tested." The first resembles those who earned anger (al-maghdubi 'alayhim), who know the truth and act contrary to it, and the second resembles those who went astray (al-dallin), who act without knowledge.

Concerning the description of Imam Ahmad: how patient he was regarding the world, and how alike he was to those who came before him! Innovations came to him and he repelled them, and the world came to him and he refused it. Such is the condition of the leaders of the pious, whom Allah, Exalted, described in His Book with His saying: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24]. So by patience desires are abandoned, and by certainty doubts are repelled, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿and they counselled one another to truth and counselled one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3], and His saying, Exalted: ﴿And remember Our servants Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, possessors of strength and vision﴾ [Sad: 45].

It is reported in some mursal narrations: "Indeed Allah loves the piercing insight at the arrival of doubts, and loves complete reason at the descent of desires." His saying, Exalted, ﴿So you have enjoyed your share﴾ is an allusion to following desires, which is the disease of the sinners. And His saying ﴿and you have plunged as they plunged﴾ is an allusion to doubts, which is the disease of the innovators, the people of whims and of disputes. And these two frequently combine, for you rarely find one whose belief is corrupt without the corruption of his belief appearing in his action. The intended meaning is that Allah informed that in this Ummah there are those who enjoy their share as those before them enjoyed their share, and who plunge as they plunged; and that for them is the same blame and threat as for those before them. Then He urged them to analogy and reflection upon those who came before them, saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Ibrahim, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their Messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah was not to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70].

So reflect on the soundness of this analogy and its benefit regarding what the ruling was attached to, and that the original case and the derived case are equal in the meaning to which the punishment is attached, and He reinforced this, as has preceded, by a kind of greater priority (awla), namely the intensity of strength, the abundance of wealth and children. So if it is not impossible for Allah to punish the stronger of them for his sin, how could it be impossible for Him to punish one who is weaker than him? From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and bring after you whatever He wills, just as He produced you from the offspring of another people﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. This is a clear analogy: He, glory be to Him, says: If I will, I can remove you and substitute others, as I removed those before you and substituted you. It mentions the four pillars of analogy: the effective cause of the ruling, which is the generality and perfection of His will; the ruling, which is His removing them and bringing others; the original case, which is what came before; and the derived case, who are those addressed.

From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 39]. He informed that those who denied before them are an original case by which one takes lesson, and the derived case is their own selves. So when they are equal in the meaning, they are equal in the outcome. From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a Messenger﴾ ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger, so We seized him with a severe seizing﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15-16]. He, glory be to Him, informed that He sent Musa to Pharaoh, and that Pharaoh disobeyed His Messenger, so He seized him with a severe seizing. Thus whoever of you disobeys Muhammad (ﷺ) [will face the same]. This is very abundant in the Qur'an, and its door has been opened for you.

As for qiyas al-dalalah (analogy by indication), it is the joining of the original case and the derived case by means of the effective cause and what necessarily accompanies it. From this is His saying (p-189), Exalted: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revives it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾ [Fussilat: 39]. He, glory be to Him, guided His servants by what He showed them of revival, which they verified and witnessed, to the revival which they deemed far-fetched. That is an analogy of revival upon revival, and considering a thing by its counterpart. The effective cause that necessitates it is the generality of His power, glory be to Him, and the perfection of His wisdom, and the revival of the earth is the indicator of the cause. From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and He revives the earth after its death. And thus you will be brought out﴾ [al-Rum: 19].

He indicated the like by means of the like, and brought one of the two very close to the other by the word "bringing out," meaning: you will be brought out from the earth alive as the living is brought out of the dead and the dead out of the living. From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected? ﴾ ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted? ﴾ ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned﴾ ﴿And made of him two sexes, male and female﴾ ﴿Is not that One Able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36-40]. So He, glory be to Him, explained the manner of creation and the varying states of the water in the womb until it became from it the two spouses, male and female. That is a sign of the existence of a Creator capable of whatever He wills. And He, glory be to Him, alerted His servants to what He produced in the despicable, humble drop, of stages, and His driving it through the levels of perfection, from one level to a higher one, until it became a sound human being in the best form and proportion. On that basis, it is not fitting for Him to leave this human being neglected, idle and unemployed, neither commanding him nor forbidding him, nor placing him in His servitude. He drove him through the levels of perfection from the time he was a drop until he became a sound human being. Likewise, He drives him through the levels of his perfection, stratum after stratum and state after state, until he becomes a neighbour of His in His abode, enjoying the kinds of bliss, looking upon His Face, and hearing His speech... to the end of the words of Ibn al-Qayyim. For he extended the mention of examples in this manner, and we have not mentioned all of his words, fearing tedious prolixity. What we have mentioned of his words is an alert to what we have not mentioned.

He also spoke about qiyas al-shabah (analogy by resemblance), and said regarding it:

As for qiyas al-shabah (analogy by resemblance), Allah, glory be to Him, related it only about the falsifiers. From it is His saying, Exalted, reporting about the brothers of Yusuf that when they found the cup in the bag of their brother, they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before﴾ [Yusuf: 77]. They did not join the derived case and the original case by an effective cause or its indicator. Rather, they attached one of them to the other without any joining indicator except the mere resemblance between him and Yusuf. They said: "This one is analogized to his brother, between them there is resemblance in many respects: that one stole, so this one too." This is joining by empty resemblance, and analogy by a bare form devoid of the effective cause that requires equality. It is a corrupt analogy, and the equality in the kinship of brotherhood is not an effective cause for equality in theft even if it were true, nor is there any indicator of equality in it, so the joining is for a type of resemblance empty of the cause and its indicator.

Then he mentioned other examples of corrupt analogy by resemblance, in the verses indicating that the disbelievers denied the Messengers by analogy of resemblance, when they likened them to humans and claimed that this resemblance prevents their prophethood. Such as His saying, Exalted, about the disbelievers, that they said: ﴿We do not see you except as a human like us﴾ [Hud: 27], and His saying, Exalted, about them: ﴿This is not but a human like you, who eats of what you eat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33], and other verses. The similarity between the Messengers and others in all being human does not necessitate equality between them in negating prophethood from all of them. When they said to the Messengers: ﴿You are not but humans like us﴾ [Yasin: 15], the Messengers answered them: ﴿We are not but humans like you, but Allah bestows favour upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [Ibrahim: 11]. The disbelievers' analogy of the Messengers to all other humans regarding the absence of prophethood is an analogy whose invalidity is manifest, because the actual reality of distinction and preference, and of making some humans noble and some base, some subordinate and some leader, some king and some common, refutes this analogy, as the Messengers' answer mentioned just above indicated. His saying, Exalted, points to this: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the worldly life and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]. These examples of analogy by resemblance contain no attribute suitable either essentially or incidentally. Therefore they are invalid.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned that all the parables (amthal) in the Qur'an are sound analogies of resemblance, because the reality of a parable (mithl) is the comparison of one thing with another in its ruling, and bringing the intelligible (ma'qul) close to the perceptible (mahsus), or one of two perceptible things close to the other, and considering one of them in light of the other. Then he listed the Qur'anic parables one by one, showing this in each of them, and he extended his discussion on that, excelling and benefiting.

He said at the end of his discourse: They said: this is some of what the Qur'an contains of illustration (tamthil), analogy (qiyas), combining (jam'), distinguishing (farq), consideration of causes ('ilal), and meanings, and their connection with their rulings, both as causal influence (ta'thir) and as evidence (istidlal). They said: Allah, glorified is He, has struck the parables and varied them, in decree (qadar) and in law (shar'), in wakefulness and in sleep, and He directed His servants to draw lessons (i'tibar) from that, and their passing from a thing to its counterpart, and their reasoning from the like to the like. Indeed, this is the basis of the interpretation of dreams (ibarat al-ru'ya), which is a part of the parts of prophethood and a type of revelation, for it is built upon analogy, illustration, and considering the intelligible in light of the perceptible.

Do you not see that garments in interpretation are like shirts, indicating religion; so whatever is in them of length or shortness, or cleanliness or filthiness, is in the religion. Just as the Prophet (ﷺ) interpreted the shirt as religion and knowledge, and the common element between them is that each of them covers its wearer and beautifies him among people.

From this is the interpretation of milk as natural disposition (fitrah), because in each of them there is nourishment that brings about life and complete growth, and that when the child is left to his natural disposition he does not turn away from milk; he is naturally inclined to prefer it over anything else. Likewise is the fitrah of Islam upon which Allah created mankind.

From this is the interpretation of cows as people of religion and goodness through whom the earth is cultivated, just as the cow is likewise, with its lack of harm and abundance of good, and the earth and its people's need for it; for this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw cows being slaughtered, that was a slaughtering among his companions.

From that is the interpretation of sowing and tilling as work, because the worker is a sower of good and evil, and what he has sown must come out for him, just as the crop of what the sower has sown comes out for the sower. So the world is a field, deeds are the seed, and the Day of Resurrection is the day of the sprouting and harvesting of the crop.

From that is the interpretation of cut, propped-up wood as hypocrites, and the common element between them is that the hypocrite has no spirit, no shade, and no fruit, so he is in the position of wood that is likewise; for this reason Exalted is He likened the hypocrites to propped-up pieces of wood, because they are bodies empty of faith and goodness. And in their being propped up there is another subtle point: when wood is put to use, it is placed in a roof, a wall, or other places of benefit; and as long as it is left empty and unused, it is propped up, some of it against others, so He likened the hypocrites to wood in the state in which it is not benefited from... to the end of his discourse. He mentioned many things from the expressions of dream interpretation, excelling and benefiting, and all of them return to considering the counterpart by its counterpart, and all of that clearly indicates that the counterpart of truth is truth and the counterpart of falsehood is falsehood.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: This is the law of Allah, His decree, His revelation, His reward and His punishment; all of it stands upon this principle, which is attaching the counterpart to the counterpart and considering the like by the like. For this reason the Lawgiver mentions the causes, the influential attributes, and the meanings that are considered in the decreed, legislated and retributive rulings, so as to indicate by that the attachment of the ruling to them wherever they are found, their requiring their rulings, and their not being separated from them except by an impediment that opposes their requirement and necessitates the non-effect of their consequences, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 4]; ﴿That is because when Allah alone is invoked, you disbelieve﴾ [Ghafir: 12]; ﴿That is because you took the signs of Allah in mockery﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 35]; ﴿That is because you used to rejoice in the earth without right and because you used to exult﴾ [40]; ﴿That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His pleasure, so He made their deeds fruitless﴾ [Muhammad: 28]; ﴿That is because they said to those who disliked what Allah revealed, "We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾ [Muhammad: 26]; ﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you﴾ [41].

Causation has come in the Noble Book sometimes with "bi" (by/because of), sometimes with "li" (for), sometimes with "anna" (that), sometimes with a combination of them, sometimes with "kay" (so that), sometimes with "min ajl" (because of), sometimes with the ordering of the consequent upon the condition, sometimes with "fa" indicating causality, sometimes with the ordering of the ruling upon the attribute that necessitates it, sometimes with "lamma" (when/since), sometimes with the emphatic "anna", sometimes with "la'alla" (perhaps/so that), and sometimes with the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). The first is as already mentioned; the "li" is as His saying: ﴿That is so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97]; and "an" as His saying: ﴿Lest you say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾ [al-An'am: 156]. Then it was said: the estimate is "lest you say," and it was said: "out of dislike that you say." "An" with "li" is as His saying: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165]. Most of this type occurs in negation, so reflect upon it.

"Kay":
• as His saying: ﴿So that it will not be a perpetual circulation﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], with the condition and consequence;
• as His saying: ﴿And if you are patient and fear Allah, their plot will not harm you at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120], with "fa";
• as His saying: ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 139]; ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a overwhelming seizure﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10]; ﴿So Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger, and We seized him with a severe seizure﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]; and the ordering of the ruling upon the attribute:
• as His saying: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15];
• and His saying: ﴿Allah will raise those who believe among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 11];
• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of the reformers﴾ [al-A'raf: 170]; ﴿And We do not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ [Yusuf: 56]; ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾ [Yusuf: 52]; and "lamma":
• as His saying: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them﴾ [43]; ﴿So when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ [al-A'raf: 166]; and the emphatic "inna":
• as His saying: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77]; ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾ [21]; and "la'alla":
• as His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]; ﴿Perhaps you will reason﴾ [2]; ﴿Perhaps you will remember﴾ [24]; and the object of purpose:
• as His saying: ﴿And there is not for anyone with Him any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High, and he is going to be pleased﴾ [al-Layl: 19-21].
That is: he did not do that as a repayment for anyone's favor among the people, but he did it seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. "Min ajl" is as His saying: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾ [5].

(p-193) The Prophet (ﷺ) has mentioned the causes of rulings and the influential attributes in them, so as to indicate their connection with them, and their extension with the extension of their attributes and causes:
• as his saying concerning date wine: "A good date and pure water";
• and his saying: "Permission was only prescribed because of the sight";
• and his saying: "I only forbade you because of the crowd (al-daffah)";
• and his saying concerning the cat: "It is not impure; it is among those who go around you and the female ones who go around";  and his forbidding the covering of the head of the muhrim whose camel broke his neck, and his bringing near of perfume;
• and his saying: "Indeed he will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection reciting the talbiyah";
• and his saying: "If you do that, you will sever your kinship," mentioned as a reason for his prohibition of marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt.
• and the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation. Say, "It is harm, so keep away from women during menstruation"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222];
• and His saying concerning wine and gambling: ﴿Shaytan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91].
And his saying ﷺ when he was asked about selling fresh dates for dried dates: "Does fresh dates decrease when it dries?" They said: "Yes." So he forbade it. And his saying: "Two should not confer privately without a third, for that would grieve him." And his saying: "If a fly falls into the vessel of one of you, dip it, for in one of its wings is a disease and in the other is a cure, and it protects itself with the wing that has the disease." And his saying: "Indeed Allah and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of donkeys, for it is filth." He said, when asked about touching the private part, whether it invalidates ablution: "Is it not but a part of you?" And his saying concerning the daughter of Hamzah: "She is not lawful for me; she is the daughter of my brother through fosterage." And his saying concerning charity: "It is not lawful for the family of Muhammad; it is only the filth of people." The Prophet (ﷺ) brought the rulings near to his community by mentioning their counterparts and causes, and he set forth parables for them... to the end of his discourse.

Analogies that the Prophet (ﷺ) made have been mentioned in it, among them the analogy of kissing to rinsing the mouth in the hadith of Umar mentioned earlier, and the analogy of the debt of Allah to the debt of a human being in the obligation of making up. We have already covered this fully, as well as what precedes it, in Surah al-Isra'.

Among them is the analogical reasoning of the reverse (qiyas al-'aks) in the hadith: "Does one of us fulfill his desire and have a reward for it?" He said: "Tell me, if he placed it in what is unlawful, would he have a burden?" We have already covered this fully in Surah al-Tawbah.

Among them is the story of the man whose wife gave birth to a black boy; we have already covered that fully in Surah al-Isra'.

Among them is the hadith of the woman with istihadah, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) analogized the blood of the vein, which is the blood of istihadah, to other bloods of veins that are not menstruation. All of this indicates that attaching the counterpart to the counterpart is part of the Sharia, with no opponent to it, as the Zahiriyyah and those who follow them claim.
