He said, may He be exalted, in this noble verse, that He subjected the mountains, meaning He made them submissive, and subjected the birds to glorify [God] along with Dawud (David). What He mentioned, may He be exalted, in this noble verse, about His subjecting the birds and mountains to glorify [God] along with His Prophet Dawud, He explained in another place, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud a bounty from Us. O mountains, echo [the praises] with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. As for His saying "echo with him," it means repeat the glorification along with him. "And the birds" means: and We called the birds to repeat the glorification with him in the same way. As for the view of one who said that "echo with him" means "travel with him," and that ta'wib (echoing) means the travel of the day, it is baseless, as you can see. And as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength. Indeed, he was constantly turning back [to God]. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] with him at evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered [to him], all turning back to Him﴾ [Sad: 17–18].

The verified position is that the glorification of the mountains and birds along with the mentioned Dawud is genuine glorification, because Allah, may He be exalted, gives them perceptions by which they glorify, perceptions that He Himself knows and we do not know. As He said: (p-232) ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]. He also said, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split and water issues from them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. And He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari that the trunk upon which the Prophet (ﷺ) used to deliver the sermon, when he moved from it to the pulpit, emitted a moaning sound. It is also established in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me with salam before I was sent as a prophet. Indeed, I still know it now." Similar examples are numerous. The established principle among scholars is that the texts of the Book and the Sunnah may not be diverted from their apparent, immediately understood meaning except by a proof to which one must return. Tasbih (glorification) linguistically means distancing from evil, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it means declaring Allah, may He be exalted, free of everything unbefitting His perfection and majesty.

Al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on this verse, ﴿And We subjected the mountains with Dawud﴾ [al-Anbiya': 79], that it means: We made them such that they obey him when he commands them to glorify [God]. The apparent meaning is that His saying "and We were doers" emphasizes His saying "And We subjected the mountains with Dawud, glorifying, and the birds" [al-Anbiya': 79]. The reason for this emphasis is that the subjecting of the mountains and their glorification is a wondrous matter that goes beyond custom, and is liable to be denied by the disbelieving and ignorant.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And We were doers" means: We were capable of doing this. It was also said: We used to do such things for the prophets. Both of these statements, which he mentioned, are clearly baseless, because interpreting "We were doers" as "We were capable" is far-fetched, and there is no proof for it, just as there is no proof for the other, as you can see.

Abu Hayyan said: "And We were doers" means: doing these wonders of subjecting the mountains, their glorification, and the birds, for whomever We single out for Our honor. End of quotation. The most evident of these, in my view, is what has preceded, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 80:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We taught him the making of chain-mail for you, to protect you from your violence. So will you not be grateful?﴾.

The pronoun in His saying "and We taught him" refers back to Dawud (David). The meaning of the word "labus" (chain-mail, armour) is the craft of making coats of mail (durū') and weaving them. The evidence that the meaning of "labus" in the verse is coats of mail is that He followed it with His saying: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80], meaning: so that he may guard and shield some of you from the violence of others, because the coat of mail protects its wearer from the harm of sword blows and of arrows and spears, as is well known. This meaning has been made clear by His saying: ﴿And We made iron soft for him, [saying]: Make full coats of mail and measure well the links﴾ [Saba: 10-11]. His saying "Make full coats of mail" means: make coats of mail that are full (covering) from the iron that We made soft for you.

Al-sard (the weaving of the mail) is the weaving of the coat of mail. It is also called al-zard. From the first usage is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

"Upon them both are two woven coats, which Dawud decided upon, or which the Tubba' made as full coats."

And from the second is the saying of another:

"We feed them with sharp swords, with which we cut what every armourer (zarrad) had sewn for them."

By "zarrad" he means the maker of coats of mail. His saying "and measure well the links" means: make the rings and the rivets in your weaving of the coat of mail in proportionate measures, so that you do not make the rivet too thin, lest it break, nor join some rings to others loosely, nor make it excessively thick so that it cuts through the ring. Once you know that "labus" in the verse means coats of mail, know that the Arabs use "labus" for coats of mail, as in the verse. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Upon them are lions, lean, whose coats of mail are full, white, which arrows cannot pierce."

His saying "full" (sawabigh) means full coats of mail. And the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"Lofty of nose, heroes, whose labus in battle are coats of mail woven by Dawud."

By "labus" which he expressed as "sarabil" (coats), he means coats of mail. The Arabs also use "labus" for all weapons, whether a coat of mail, a jawshan (breastplate), a sword or a spear. From its use for a spear is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali describing a spear:

"And with me is a labus against the fierce one, as if it were a horn on the forehead of a bull with herds, startled."

The Arabs also use "labus" for everything that is worn. From this is the saying of Bayhas:

"Wear for every state its garment (labus), whether its bliss or its hardship."

What He mentions here of the favour upon creation by teaching him the craft of coats of mail, so that they may protect themselves with them from the violence of weapons, has already been explained in surah "al-Nahl" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And coats of mail that protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl: 81].

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿So will you not be grateful?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80], the apparent meaning is that the interrogative form here is intended as a command. Among the uses of the interrogative in the sense of a command in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], meaning: desist. Therefore 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We have desisted, O Lord." And His saying: ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: Have you submitted?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20], meaning: submit. It has been established in the science of rhetoric (fann al-ma'ani) that among the meanings conveyed by the interrogative form is the command, as we have mentioned.

His saying "grateful" (shakirun): the gratitude of the servant to his Lord is that he seeks help from His blessings in obeying Him, and the gratitude of the Lord to His servant is that He rewards him with a generous reward for his little deed. The root "shakara" does not generally take a direct object except with the preposition "li-" (to/for), and taking it directly without "li-" is rare. From this is the saying of Abu Nukhaylah:

"I thank you, for gratitude is a rope of piety, and not everyone to whom you have given a favour repays it."

In His saying "li-tuhsinakum" there are three seven-canonical readings. Most of the seven read it "liyuhsinakum" with the yā' (third person), and on this reading the subject pronoun refers either to Dawud or to the labus, since its masculine form is permissible by consideration of the meaning of what is worn of coats of mail. Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read "lituhsinakum" with the tā' (second person feminine form), and on this reading the subject pronoun refers to the labus, which is feminine, or to the craft mentioned in His saying "the making of chain-mail." Shu'bah from 'Asim read "linuhsinakum" with the nūn indicating majesty, and on this reading the matter is clear.

The commentary's opening Qur'anic citation:

﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind, violently blowing, running by his command to the land which We had blessed. And We are ever Knowing of all things.﴾

His saying, ﴿And to Sulayman the wind﴾ [al-Anbiya: 81] is coordinated with the object of "and We subjected" in his saying, ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79]. That is: and We subjected the wind to Sulayman while it was violently blowing, meaning intensely gusting. It is said: "The wind became violent" (ʿasafat al-rīḥ), meaning it grew strong. So it is a wind that is ʿāṣif and ʿaṣūf. In the dialect of the Banu Asad, it is "aʿṣafat," so it is muʿṣif and muʿṣifa. We have already cited some of its Arabic evidence in the surah of al-Isra'.

His saying, ﴿running by his command﴾, means: it obeys him and runs to the place to which he commands it. What He mentions in this verse about the subjection of the wind to Sulayman, and that it runs by his command, He has explained in another place, and He added the measure of its speed, in His saying: ﴿And to Sulayman the wind: its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ (p-235) [Saba': 12], and His saying: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind, running gently by his command wherever he intended﴾ [Sad: 36].

Note

Know that in these verses we have mentioned there are two well-known questions:

The first: it may be asked: God described the wind mentioned here in surah al-Anbiya' as violent, meaning intensely gusting, and described it in surah Sad as running gently by His command. A violent wind is not the same as one that runs gently.

The second question: here in surah al-Anbiya' He restricted its running to [being] to the land which He blessed for all the worlds, whereas in surah Sad He said: ﴿running gently by his command wherever he intended﴾ [Sad: 36]. His saying "wherever he intended" indicates generality regarding the places to which he wishes to go by means of the wind. So "wherever he intended" means wherever he willed, as Mujahid said. Ibn al-A'rabi said: the Arabs say: "He hit the right thing (aṣāba al-ṣawāb), and missed the answer (akhṭa'a al-jawāb)," meaning he intended the right thing and missed the answer. From this is the saying of the poet:

"He hit the speech but could not, so he missed the answer at the joint."

Al-Qurtubi said this. It is also reported from Ru'bah that two men from among the people of the language set out to ask him about the meaning of "aṣāba." He came out to them and said: "Where do you aim (tuṣībān)?" They said: "This is our objective," and they returned.

As for the answer to the first question, it is in two ways. The first: it is violent at some times and gentle and mild at others, according to need. For example, it blows violently at the beginning, until it lifts the carpet on which Sulayman and his soldiers are, and when it has risen, it carries him gently wherever he intends.

The second answer is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. He said: If you ask: this wind is described with violence at one time and with gentleness at another; how is this reconciled? I say: in itself it was gentle and pleasant, like a breeze, but when it passed by his throne it carried him away in a short time, as He said: ﴿its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾. So the combination of the two matters was that it was gentle in itself and violent in its action, along with its obedience to Sulayman and its blowing according to what he wills and decides. End of the relevant point.

As for the answer to the second question: His saying "wherever he intended" indicates that it runs by his command to wherever he wishes from the regions of the earth. And His saying ﴿to the land which We have blessed (p-236)﴾ [Sad: 36] — because his dwelling is there, and it is al-Sham (Greater Syria), so it returns him to al-Sham. Accordingly, His saying "wherever he intended" refers to the situation of going, and His saying ﴿to the land which We have blessed﴾ refers to the situation of returning to the place of residence. Thus the direction is separated and the difficulty disappears.

Nabigha of the Dhubyan [tribe] said:

"Except Sulayman, when God said to him: 'Stand in the wilderness and set its boundaries away from the wastes,
And tame the jinn; I have indeed permitted them to build Tadmur with cut stones and pillars.'"

Tadmur is a town in al-Sham. This indicates that al-Sham was the place of his residence, as is well known.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 82:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And of the devils were those who dove for him and did other work than that; and We were guardians over them.﴾ It is in a position of accusative case (nasb) by conjunction ('atf) with the object (ma'mul) of "We subjected" (sakhkharna), meaning: "And We subjected to him those devils who dove for him." It has also been said that "min" (of) is the subject (mubtada'), and the preposition phrase before it is its predicate (khabar).

In this noble verse, Exalted is He mentions that He subjected to Solomon those devils who dove for him, meaning they dove for him in the seas and extracted from them precious jewels, such as pearls and coral. Al-ghawš (diving) is descending beneath the water, and al-ghawwas (diver) is one who dives into the sea to extract pearls and the like from it. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha Dhubyani:

"Or a pearl of the oyster kind, whose diver is delighted; whenever he sees it, he exclaims and prostrates."

In this noble verse, Exalted is He also mentions that the devils subjected to him do other work besides that diving mentioned, meaning such as building cities and palaces, making prayer niches (mahareeb), statues, large basins (jifan), and great fixed cooking pots (qudur rasiyat), and other amazing crafts.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿and We were guardians over them﴾ means: protecting them from deviating from His command, or from altering or changing, or from any corruption arising in what they are subjected to. These three matters included in this noble verse are explained elsewhere, such as:

• His saying regarding diving and building alike: ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver﴾ [Sad: 37], and so on.

• His saying regarding work other than diving: ﴿And of the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord﴾ [Saba: 12].

• His saying: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of prayer niches, statues, basins like reservoirs, and great fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba: 13].

• And as His saying regarding their being guarded from deviating from His command: ﴿And whoever of them deviates from Our command, We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [Saba: 12] (p-237)

• And His saying: ﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾ [Sad: 38].

The description of the carpet, the description of the wind carrying it for him, and the description of Solomon's hosts of jinn, mankind and birds are all mentioned extensively in the books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and we have not lengthened the discussion of them in this blessed commentary.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 21, verse 83:**

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and removed what was upon him of adversity, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾

The apparent meaning is that the phrase "wa-Ayyub" (and Ayyub) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted, in Surah Sad: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ [38:41]

In these two noble verses, Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to mention Ayyub when he called out to his Lord, saying: ﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ [21:83]. Allah responded to him, removed from him all the adversity that was upon him, gave him his family, and gave him the like of them with them, as a mercy from Him, the Exalted, and as a reminder for the worshippers, meaning those who worship Allah, because they are the ones who benefit from the reminder.

The meaning mentioned here is also mentioned in Surah Sad, in the words of Allah: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment"﴾, up to His words: ﴿as a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [38:41–43]. The adversity that touched Ayyub, for which he called out to his Lord so that He would remove it from him, was a trial that afflicted his body, his family and his wealth. When Allah willed to remove the adversity from him, He commanded him to strike the ground with his foot, and he did so, and a spring of water gushed forth for him. He bathed in it, and everything of adversity on the outside of his body was removed, and he drank from it, and everything within his body was removed. Allah, the Exalted, alluded to this in His words: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾ [38:42].

As for what He mentioned in Surah al-Anbiya' — that He gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Him and a reminder for whoever worships Him — He explained it in Surah Sad in His words: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [38:43]. His words in al-Anbiya', ﴿and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ [21:84], together with His words in Sad, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [38:43], contain clear evidence that the people of sound intellects, free from defects of deficiency, are the ones who worship Allah alone and obey Him. This supports the view of some scholars that if a person bequeaths some of his wealth to "the most intelligent of people," that bequest is to be spent on the most pious of people and those most devoted to obeying Allah, the Exalted, because they are the "people of understanding" (ulu al-albab), meaning those of correct intellects, free from defect. (p-238)

**A Note**

In these mentioned verses there is a well-known question, which is: the statement of Ayyub mentioned in al-Anbiya' in His words, ﴿when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me"﴾, and in Sad in His words, ﴿when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment"﴾, seems to indicate that he became impatient with the illness and complained of it, while Allah's words about him, ﴿Indeed, We found him patient; an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one who turned back in repentance﴾ [38:44], indicate the perfection of his patience.

The answer is that what came from Ayyub was supplication and a display of his poverty and need before his Lord, not complaint or impatience.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on this noble verse: "His saying, ﴿adversity has touched me﴾, was not impatience, because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾. Rather, that was a supplication from him. Impatience is in complaining to creatures, not to Allah, the Exalted, and supplication does not contradict contentment." Al-Tha'labi said: "I heard our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I attended a gathering crowded with jurists and men of letters in the palace of the ruler, and I was asked about this noble verse, after they had agreed that the words of Ayyub were a complaint, and Allah the Exalted had said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾. I said: This is not a complaint, but it was a supplication, as is shown by His words ﴿So We answered him﴾, and an answer follows a supplication, not a complaint. They approved of this and were pleased with it." And al-Junayd was asked about this noble verse, and he said: "He made him aware of his need to ask, so that He might bestow upon him the generosity of giving." End of quotation.

The supplication of Ayyub mentioned here, which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Anbiya' without attributing the touching of adversity to Satan, in His words ﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, and which He mentioned in Surah Sad where He attributed it to Satan in His words ﴿Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment﴾ — the word "nusb" (hardship), in all the recitations, means fatigue and difficulty, and "adhab" (torment) means pain. Attributing the hardship and pain that befell him to Satan in this Surah Sad is a well-known strong problem, because Allah mentioned in verses of His Book that Satan has no authority over prophets of noble standing like Ayyub:

• As in His words: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [16:99–100].

• And His words, the Exalted: ﴿And he had no authority over them﴾ [34:21], up to the end of the verse.

• And His words, the Exalted, affirming this: ﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾ [14:22].

• And His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, over My servants you have no authority, except those of the deviators who follow you﴾ [15:42].

The scholars have several answers to this problem, among them what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. He said:

"If you say: Why did he attribute it to Satan, when it is not permissible that He would give him power over His prophets to fulfil his desire of exhausting and tormenting them? And if he had been able to do that, he would not have left a righteous person without afflicting and destroying him. And it has been repeated in the Qur'an that he has no power except whispering alone?

I say: Since his whispering to him and his obedience to him in what he whispered were a cause of the hardship and torment that Allah touched him with, he attributed it to him. He observed good manners in this, in that he did not attribute it to Allah in his supplication, although He is the doer of it, and none is able to do it except Him. It was also said: He meant what Satan used to whisper to him during his illness, magnifying the calamity that had befallen him and urging him toward aversion and impatience, so he turned to Allah, the Exalted, asking Him to suffice him against that by removing the calamity, or by granting him success in repelling and warding it off through beautiful patience." End of quotation.

It was also narrated that three of the believers used to visit him, and one of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into his heart that Allah does not test the righteous prophets. It was also mentioned as the cause of his affliction that a man sought his help against an oppressor, and he did not help him. It was also said: his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not fight him. It was also said: he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth. End of quotation.

Among the answers is what a group of exegetes mentioned: that Allah gave Satan power over his wealth and family as a trial for Ayyub, so Satan destroyed his wealth and children. Then He gave him power over his body as a trial for him, so he blew into his body a breath from which it caught fire, and boils appeared on his body. He scratched them with his nails until they bled, then with potsherds until his flesh fell away. Allah preserved his heart and tongue. (Most of this is from the Isra'iliyyat, narratives of Jewish and Christian origin.) Giving Satan power over his body, wealth and family for the sake of trial is possible, and it is closer to the truth than giving him power over him by making him do what is not fitting, such as flattering the king mentioned above, or failing to aid the one who called for help, and other matters that the exegetes mention. They have mentioned here a long story that includes the trial he went through and its duration. (All of that is from the Isra'iliyyat.) We have mentioned here only a little of it.

The most that the Qur'an indicates is that Allah tested His prophet Ayyub, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, and that he called out to Him, so He answered him, removed from him every adversity, and granted him his family and the like of them with them. And Ayyub attributed (p-240) that in Surah Sad to Satan. It is possible that Allah gave Satan power over his body, wealth and family as a trial, so that his beautiful patience would be manifest, and so that he would have praiseworthy well-being in this world and the Hereafter, and everything that he had lost would be returned to him. Allah knows best. This does not contradict the fact that Satan has no authority over the likes of Ayyub, because giving power over family, wealth and body is of the kind of causes from which human ailments arise, such as sickness. Such things happen to prophets: they are afflicted by illness, the death of family, and the loss of wealth, for various reasons. There is no barrier to the view that the sum of those causes includes Satan being given power over these things as a trial. We have already explained in Surah Ta-Ha the permissibility of illnesses and human influences befalling prophets.

As for Allah's words to His prophet Ayyub in Surah Sad: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it and do not break your oath﴾ [38:44], the exegetes said concerning it: He had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes, so Allah commanded him to take a bundle (dhighth) and strike her with it, in order to be released from his oath. The "dhighth" is a small bundle of grass, or basil, or the like. The meaning is that he takes a bundle containing one hundred stalks and strikes her with it in a single blow, and thereby he is released from his oath. We have already presented, in Surah al-Kahf, the argument from the verse ﴿and do not break your oath﴾ [38:44] that a delayed exception (istithna') is of no benefit, for if it were beneficial, Allah would have said to Ayyub: "Say, if Allah wills," so that this would be an exception in your oath.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 87 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree (any hardship) upon him. Then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from the distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾

That is: remember Dhu'l-Nun. Al-Nun means the fish (al-hut). "Dhu" here means "companion" (sahib). So His saying "Dhu'l-Nun" means "the companion of the fish," as Allah made clear in al-Qalam, in His saying: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ (68:48). He attributed him to the fish because it swallowed him, as the Exalted said: ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ (37:142).

As for His saying: ﴿thinking that We would not decree upon him﴾ (21:87), there are two interpretations of it which do not contradict one another:

The first: the meaning is "We would not decree upon him," i.e., We would not constrict him within the belly of the fish. An example of using qadara in the sense of "constricted" in the Qur'an is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and constricts it﴾ (13:26), i.e., He constricts provision for whom He wills. And His saying: ﴿Let the one of abundance spend from his abundance, and whoever has his provision constricted (qudira 'alayhi rizquhu), let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ (65:7). So His saying "whoever has his provision constricted" means whoever has his provision constricted.

The second: the meaning of "We would not decree upon him" (21:87) is "We would not ordain that for him." Accordingly it is from qadar and qada'. Qadara with the light (unaugmented) form comes in the sense of qaddara (the doubled form). From it is His saying: ﴿So the waters met for a matter already decreed (qad qudira)﴾ (54:12), i.e., Allah decreed it. From it is the saying of the poet, which Tha'lab recited as evidence for this:

"Those evenings of the sanctuary will not return to us, ever, as long as the green acacia leafs,
Nor will that time which has passed return. Blessed are You; whatever You decree (taqdiru), gratitude befalls you."

The Arabs say: qadara Allah lakal-khayra yaqdiruhu qadran, like daraba yadribu and nasara yansuru, meaning qaddarahu laka taqdiran (Allah decreed good for you). From it, according to the more correct of the two opinions, is "Laylat al-Qadr" (the Night of Decree), because Allah decrees matters in it, as He said: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾ (44:4). Al-qadar with a fatha and al-qadr with a sukun mean what Allah decrees of qada'. From it is the saying of Hudhba ibn al-Khashram:

"Ah, my people, for the calamities and the decree, and for a matter that a man comes upon from where he does not know."

As for the saying of whoever said that "lan naqdira 'alayhi" (21:87) is from qudrah (power), that is clearly false, because the Prophet of Allah Yunus did not doubt Allah's power over all things, as is not hidden.

His saying in this noble verse: "in anger" (mughadiban), i.e., in a state of being angry with his people. The form of mufa'alah in it means: he angered them by departing from them and their fear of the descent of punishment upon them, and they angered him when he invited them to Allah for a period and they did not respond to him, so he threatened them with punishment. Then he left among them in the manner of the prophets when punishment descends, before Allah had permitted him to leave. This is what Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr. He also said: it has been said that the meaning of "mughadiban" is ghadbān (angry), and it is of the mufa'alah form which does not require mutual participation, like 'aqabtu al-lis (I punished the thief) and safartu (I travelled). End of quote.

Know that the saying of whoever said "mughadiban" means "angry with his Lord," as narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and this was said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and chosen by al-Tabari and al-Qutaybi, and al-Mahdawi found it good, must be understood according to the meaning of the first opinion, i.e., angry for the sake of his Lord. Al-Qurtubi said after mentioning this opinion from those we mentioned: al-Nahhas said: "Sometimes whoever does not know the language denies this, and it is a correct statement; the meaning is: angry for the sake of his Lord, as you say: I became angry for you, i.e., for your sake, and the believer becomes angry for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when He is disobeyed." End of quote. The meaning according to what was mentioned is: angry with his people for the sake of his Lord, i.e., for their disbelief in Him and their disobedience to Him. Other than this is not valid for the verse.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then He called out in the darknesses﴾, i.e., the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the night, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. "An" in His saying: ﴿that there is no god but You﴾ (21:87) is explanatory (mufassirah), and we have already clarified earlier the meaning of "an la ilaha," the meaning of "subhanaka," and the meaning of "zulm," so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

His saying: ﴿So We answered him﴾, i.e., We responded to him and saved him from the distress in which he was, in the belly of the fish. The use of istajaba in the sense of ajaba is well known in the language, and from it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi:

"And a caller called: O you who answer to generosity; then no one answered him at that moment."

What Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in this verse of the great call of His Prophet Yunus in those darknesses, and that Allah answered him and saved him from the distress, He has clarified in other places.

In some places He clarified that had he not glorified (Allah) with this great glorification, he would have remained in the belly of the fish until the Day of Resurrection and would not have come out of it. In some of them He clarified that He cast him onto the barren land while he was sick.

In some of them He clarified that he went out without permission, like the going out of a runaway slave, and that they cast lots over who would be thrown into the sea, and the lot fell upon Yunus, that he was the one to be thrown in.

In some of them He clarified that Allah overtook him with His mercy. Had He not overtaken him with it, he would have been cast onto the barren land while blameworthy; but He overtook him with it, so he was cast out not blameworthy. Allah said in al-Saffat: ﴿And indeed Yunus was among the messengers. When he fled to the laden ship, and cast lots and was among the losers, and the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy. Had he not been among those who glorify (Allah), he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected. So We cast him onto the barren land while he was sick. And We caused a gourd tree to grow over him. And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more. And they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ (37:139–148). So His saying in the mentioned verses of al-Saffat: ﴿when he fled﴾ (37:140), i.e., when he ran away, is from the saying of the Arabs: "an abiq slave" (a runaway slave); because Yunus left before his Lord had given him permission, and for this reason the name of fleeing and deserving blame was applied to him in His saying: ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾ (37:142), because mulim is the active participle of alama when one does what deserves blame. And His saying: "fasahama", i.e., he cast lots, meaning that he placed with the people of the ship the arrows of lots, so that the arrow of the one to be cast into the sea would come out. And His saying: ﴿so he was among the losers﴾, i.e., those defeated in the lot; because the arrow came out for him, the one whose companion is cast into the sea. From this is the saying of the poet:

"We slew the losers in every mountain pass, and the eyes were cooled by their killing."

And His saying: "fanabadhnahu", i.e., We cast him away, by commanding the fish to throw him onto the shore. Al-'ara' means the open desert. The saying of whoever said al-'ara' is the wide open space, or the expanse of land, or the empty place, or the surface of the earth, all return to this; and from it is the saying of the poet, who was a man from Khuza'a:

"I raised a leg whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast my garments in the open land (al-'ara')."

The tree of yaqtin is the gourd (al-dubba'). His saying: ﴿while he was sick﴾, i.e., ill because of what befell him from the fish's swallowing him. Allah said in al-Qalam: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was distressed. Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast onto the barren land while he was blameworthy. Then his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous﴾ (68:48–50). So His saying in this verse of al-Qalam, "when he called out" (68:48), i.e., he called out: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." And His saying: ﴿while he was distressed﴾ (68:48), i.e., filled with grief, as Allah said: ﴿and We saved him from the distress﴾ (21:88), and this is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. From 'Ata' and Abu Malik: "makzum" means filled with anguish. Al-Mawardi said: the difference between ghamm (grief) and karb (anguish) is that ghamm is in the heart, and karb is in the breath. It was also said that makzum means restrained, and al-kazm means restraint; from it is the saying "kazama ghaydahu" (he restrained his anger), i.e., he held back his rage, as Ibn Bahr said. It was also said: al-makzum is one seized by his kazm, which is the passage of breath, as al-Mubarrad said. End of quote from al-Qurtubi.

The verse of al-Qalam mentioned indicates that the Prophet of Allah Yunus, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, hastened to depart and to be angry with his people, and did not show the obligatory patience, as is shown by His saying addressing our Prophet ﷺ in it: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ (68:48). For His command to our Prophet ﷺ to be patient and His prohibition to him that he be like the companion of the fish is evidence that the companion of the fish did not show patience as he should. The story of Yunus, the cause of his departure and his anger with his people, is well known and mentioned in the books of tafsir. Allah has clarified in Surah Yunus that the people of Yunus believed, and their faith benefited them, unlike the other towns to which messengers were sent. That is in His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ (10:98).

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾, it indicates that no believer who is struck by anguish and grief, then supplicates to Allah, calling upon Him sincerely, is not saved by Allah from that grief, especially if he calls with this supplication of Yunus. It has come in a marfu' hadith from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the supplication of Yunus mentioned: "No Muslim has ever made this supplication to his Lord for anything except that He answered him." Related by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir, and others. The noble verse is a strong witness to this hadith, as you see; because when He mentioned that He saved Yunus, He likened to it His saving of the believers. His saying ﴿nunji al-mu'minin﴾ is a general form applying to every believer, as you see.

The majority of the seven readers, other than Ibn 'Amir and Shu'ba from 'Asim, recited ﴿wa-kadhalika nunji al-mu'minin﴾ with two nuns, the first of which is damma-ed and the second sakin, followed by a jim with kasra, lightened, then a sakin ya'. This is the present tense of the quadriliteral anja in the form af'ala, and the first nun indicates majesty. Ibn 'Amir and Shu'ba from 'Asim recited "wa-kadhalika nujjī al-mu'minin" with one nun damma-ed, followed by a jim with kasra, doubled, then a sakin ya'. In this reading it is in the form of the past tense passive of najja, the doubled form on the pattern fa''ala with gemination. In both readings there is a well-known difficulty. As for the reading of the majority, it is clear from the standpoint of Arabic grammar and there is no difficulty in it, but there is a difficulty from another standpoint: namely, that the Companions wrote this letter in the 'Uthmanic codices with one nun, so it is asked: how can it be read with two nuns when it is in the codices with one nun? As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'ba, the difficulty is from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, because najja in their reading is in the past tense passive form, so analogically the mu'minin after it should be in the nominative as the deputy subject, and likewise analogically the ya' of "najja" should be fatha-ed, not sukun-ed.

And the scholars answered this in several ways. Among them is what some of the imams mentioned, and Ibn Hisham (d. 761 AH) pointed to it in the chapter on assimilation (idgham) in his Tawdih: the original reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah, "nunajjī" with a fatha on the second nun, is the present tense of najjā (to deliver) in its doubled form, so the second nun was deleted for lightness. Or it is nunjī with a sukun on it, the present tense of anjā (to deliver), and the nun was assimilated into the jim because they share voicing (jahr), openness (infitah), and a middle position between strength and weakness, just as it was assimilated in "ijjāṣah" and "ijjānah" with a shadda on the jim in both, the original being "injāṣah" and "injānah," where the nun was assimilated into them. The ijjāṣah is the singular of ijjāṣ (apricot). In al-Qamus, he said: "al-ijjāṣ, with a kasra and a shadda, is a known fruit, a loanword, since the jim and the sad do not come together in one word. Its singular takes a ha'. Do not say injāṣ, or it is a dialectal form." End of quote. And al-ijjānah is the singular of al-ajajin (kneading troughs). In al-Tasrih, he said: it is with a fatha or a kasra on the hamza. The author of al-Fasih said: "a earthenware vessel in which dough is kneaded and washed." It is said: injānah, just as it is said injāṣah, and it is a Yemeni dialect form in both, which most scholars rejected. End of quote. These are two explanations for the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah, and on them the word "al-mu'minin" is the direct object of "nunajjī."

Another answer from the scholars regarding the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah: "nujjiya" in their reading is a past-tense verb in the passive voice, and the substitute for the subject is the verbal noun (masdar) pronoun, meaning "he delivered," i.e., the deliverance (al-injā'). On this view the verse is like the reading of one who reads "liyujza qawman" (45:14) with "yujza" in the passive, the substitute being the verbal noun pronoun, meaning "that he may recompense," i.e., the recompense. The substitution of a verbal noun for the subject, when the verb is transitive to an object, occurs rarely, as he indicated in the Khulasah with his words:

"Accept from adverbs, or from a verbal noun, or from a prepositional phrase, a substitution, being apt for it. But none of these substitutes if a direct object exists in the wording; yet it may occur."

The point of evidence from it is his words "yet it may occur." Among those who permitted this were al-Akhfash, the Kufans, and Abu 'Ubayd. Among examples of this in Arabic speech is Jarir's verse satirizing the mother of al-Farazdaq:

"Even if Qufayrah gave birth to a whelp of a dog, the dogs would have been cursed for that whelp." (Meaning: cursing itself was cursed, i.e., the cursing.)

And the verse of the rajaz poet:

"He meant by 'al-'Ulya' none but a lord, and none healed one who was astray except one who is guided."

As for the sukun on the ya' of "nujjī" on this view, it is according to the dialect of those Arabs who say "radiya" and "baqiya" with a sukun on the ya' for lightness. From this is the reading of al-Hasan, "wadhar ma baqiya mina al-riba" (2:278), with a sukun on the ya' of "baqiya." Among the evidences for that dialect is the poet's verse:

"Gray hair has dyed my locks thoroughly, and the camel urged me on to the graves."
"Would that I knew, when the Resurrection arose and they were summoned to reckoning, where the destination would be."

As for the answer regarding the reading of the majority, the evident point is that the Companions omitted the nun in the mushafs, so that the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah could agree with the mushafs because it was hidden. As for the reading of the majority, its explanation is evident and there is no difficulty in it. The utmost one can say is that they deleted a letter from the word for a benefit, while the transmission of the recitation is mutawatir verbally, with mention of the deleted letter. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 92:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects. To Us they will all return.﴾

(p-246) We have already presented the meanings of "ummah" (community) in the Qur'an in Surah Hud. The intended meaning of "ummah" here is the sharia (sacred law) and the millah (religious creed). The meaning is: indeed, this sharia of yours is one sharia, namely the tawhid of Allah in its most perfect form in every respect, the carrying out of His command, and the avoidance of His prohibitions with sincerity in that, in accordance with what He has prescribed for His creation. ﴿And I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92], i.e., Me alone. The meaning is: your religion is one and your Lord is one, so why do you differ? ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 93], i.e., they split up in the religion and became sects; among them are Jews, among them are Christians, among them are idol-worshippers, and other diverse factions.

Then, by His saying ﴿To Us they will all return﴾, He made clear that they all will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection, and He will requite them for what they did. Al-Zamakhshari said in his commentary on this noble verse, ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves﴾: the meaning is that they made the affair of their religion among themselves into pieces, just as a group distributes a thing and divides it up, so that this one has a share and that one has a share; as a metaphor for their disagreement about it and their becoming scattered sects. End of quotation.

The apparent sense of the verse is that "taqatta'a" (divided) is transitive, its object being "amrahum" (their affair), and the meaning of "taqatta'uhu" is that they made it into pieces, as we have mentioned. Al-Qurtubi said: al-Azhari said: ﴿But they divided their affair﴾, i.e., they split up regarding their affair, so "amrahum" is in the accusative by the deletion of "fi" (in). Among the uses of "ummah" in the sense of sharia and religion, as in this verse, is His saying, exalted is He, about the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23], i.e., upon a sharia, creed and religion. Of this is the saying of Nabigha Dhubyani:

"I swore an oath, leaving no doubt in your mind, and can one of a community (ummah) who is obedient commit sin?"

The meaning of his saying "and can one of a community... etc." is that the possessor of a religion does not commit sin willingly.

What He, majestic and exalted, mentioned in these two noble verses, namely that the religion is one and the Lord is one, so there is no reason for disagreement, and that they nevertheless differed or became factions, He clarified in Surah ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾, and added that every party of the differing groups rejoices in what it has. That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteousness; indeed, I am Knower of what you do﴾, ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾, ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into scriptures; every faction, in what they have, is rejoicing﴾, ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51-54]. (p-247) His saying in this verse, "zuburan" (scriptures/pieces), means pieces, like the pieces of iron and silver, i.e., their fragments. His saying ﴿every faction, in what they have, is rejoicing﴾ means: every sect of these misguided, differing, fragmented groups that split their religion into pieces rejoices in its falsehood, is content with it, and believes it to be the truth.

He, majestic and exalted, has also made clear in another place that what they rejoiced in and were content with is falsehood, as He said in Surah "al-Mu'min": ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what they had of knowledge, and there encompassed them what they had been mocking﴾, ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone and disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ [Ghafir: 83-84]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you are not of them in anything; their affair is only with Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do﴾ [al-An'am: 159].

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: "Inna hadhihi" — "hadhihi" is the subject of "inna," and its predicate is "ummatukum." His saying "ummatan wahidatan" (one community) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), as is evident.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be going into it.﴾

This verse indicates that all objects of worship, along with those who worship them, are in the Fire.

Other verses have indicated that some of those worshipped, such as ʿIsā (Jesus) and the angels, are not among the people of the Fire,

such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the son of Maryam was cited as an example﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 57]

and His saying: ﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these people worship you?"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 40]

and His saying: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord, [each] of them competing as to which of them would be nearest﴾ [al-Isra': 57], to the end of the verse.

The answer comes from two aspects:

The first: that this verse does not include the angels or ʿIsā, because it uses the word ﴿mā﴾ ("what"), which denotes non-rational beings.

Allah, may He be exalted, indicated this answer by His saying: ﴿They do not present it to you except for argument. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 58], for if they were fair, they would not have claimed that rational beings are included in a term that does not linguistically encompass them.

The second: that Allah explicitly excluded the angels and ʿIsā from this, to remove the misconception and this false argument, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us will be kept far from it﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Anbiya': 101], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me that your God is but one God; so will you not submit?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 108].

In this noble verse He used the word ﴿innamā﴾ ("only"), which, according to the majority of scholars, denotes restriction (ḥaṣr). Accordingly, it indicates that revelation is restricted to the affirmation of the Oneness of Divinity (tawḥīd al-ulūhiyyah).

Other verses have come indicating that He revealed other matters as well, such as:

His saying: ﴿Say, "It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened"﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], to the end of the verse,

and His saying: ﴿These are from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ [Hud: 49],

and His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 3], to the end of the verse.

The answer is that restricting revelation to the Oneness of Divinity is a restriction to its greatest foundation, to which all branches return, because the laws of all the prophets are included within "There is no god but Allah," since its meaning is the rejection of all rivals besides Allah in all types of worship, and the singling out of Allah with all types of worship. Thereby all commands and prohibitions, whether spoken, practical or doctrinal, are encompassed.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 100:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them therein is wheezing (zafir)﴾.

In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, mentions that the people of the Fire have therein wheezing (zafir), we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He. The most evident of the opinions concerning zafir is that it is like the first sound of a donkey, and that shahiq (the drawn-out inhaling groan) is like its last part. Allah, exalted, has clarified in other than this place that the people of the Fire have therein wheezing, and He added to that shahiq and eternal abiding, as in His saying in Hud: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is wheezing and shahiq﴾ ﴿abiding therein﴾ [verse 106].

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they therein will not hear﴾.

In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, mentions that the people of the Fire will not hear therein. He has clarified in other than this place that they will not speak and will not see,

• as in His saying in al-Isra': ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97],

• and His saying: ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:124],

• and His saying: ﴿And the word will be fulfilled against them for what they did wrong, and they will not speak﴾ [an-Naml 27:85]. Yet He, may He be glorified and exalted, has mentioned in other verses what indicates that they hear, see and speak,

• as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How clearly they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us﴾ [Maryam 19:38] to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard﴾ [as-Sajdah 32:12] to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾ [al-Kahf 18:53] to the end of the verse.

We have already explained the ways of reconciling the verses mentioned in Ta-Ha, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 101:

(p-248) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward (al-husna) has preceded from Us, they will be kept far away from it﴾.

In this noble verse, He, glorified and exalted, mentions that those for whom al-husna had preceded from Him in His knowledge, — al-husna being the feminine form of al-ahsan (the best), and it is Paradise or felicity — will be kept far away from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. He has alluded to something similar in other places, such as His saying: ﴿For those who have done good is the best (al-husna) and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26], and His saying: ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60], and similar verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels will meet them: "This is your day which you were promised."﴾

In this noble verse, He, exalted and most high, mentioned that His believing servants, for whom the good reward (al-husna) had preceded from Him, ﴿and the angels will meet them﴾ [21], meaning: they will receive them with glad tidings, and they will say to them: ﴿"This is your day which you were promised,"﴾ meaning: you were promised therein all kinds of honor and bliss. It was said: they will receive them with this at the gates of Paradise. And it was said: at the time of coming out of the graves, as has preceded.

What He, exalted and most high, mentioned regarding the angels receiving them with this, He explained in other places, such as His saying in Fussilat: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve, but rejoice in Paradise which you were promised. We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter. And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request. As a welcome from Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."﴾ [Fussilat: 30-32] And His saying in An-Nahl: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter Paradise for what you used to do."﴾ [16:32], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day We fold up the heaven like the folding of written scrolls for records﴾.

His saying: ﴿On the Day We fold up the heaven﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104] is in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿the Terror will not grieve them﴾ [21], or by His saying ﴿the angels will receive them﴾. In this noble verse, He - exalted is He - mentioned that on the Day of Resurrection He will fold up the heaven like the folding of the scroll over the records. In az-Zumar He stated explicitly that the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and that the heavens will be folded up in His right hand, in His saying: ﴿They have not measured God with His true measure. The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾ [az-Zumar: 67]. What He mentioned in this verse concerning the heavens being folded up in His right hand has also been related in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ). We have stated many times that the obligation in this matter is to let it pass as it came, to affirm it, and to believe that the attribute of the Creator is far greater than that it should resemble the attribute of the created.

The statements of the scholars concerning the meaning of His saying (p-249) ﴿like the folding of written scrolls for records﴾ return to two matters:

The first: that the sijill (scroll) is the sahifah (page), and the meaning of "lil-kutub" (for the records) is what is written in it, and the lam is in the sense of 'ala (upon), i.e., like the folding of the scroll upon what is written in it, i.e., like the folding of the page upon what is written in it. On this view, "tayy al-sijill" is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, because the sijill in this meaning is the object of the folding.

The second: that the sijill is an angel from among the angels, who is the one who folds the books of the deeds of the children of Adam when they are raised to him. It is said that he is in the third heaven, to which the guardians appointed over creation raise the deeds of the children of Adam every Thursday and Monday. Among his assistants, as they mentioned, were Harut and Marut. It is also said that he does not fold the page until its owner dies, and then he raises it and folds it until the Day of Resurrection. The statement of one who said that as-Sijill is a companion and scribe of the Prophet (ﷺ) is clearly unsound, as you see.

His saying in this noble verse "lil-kitab" was read by the majority of the Seven, except Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, as "lil-kitab" with a kasrah on the kaf and a fathah on the ta' followed by an alif, in the singular form. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "lil-kutub" with a dammah on the kaf and the ta', in the plural form. The meaning of the two readings is one, because what is meant by "al-kitab" in the singular reading is the genus of the book, which encompasses all books.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 105:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾. The view that appears most correct to me regarding this noble verse is that "the Zabur," which is the Book, is meant generically (jins al-kitab), so it includes the revealed books such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms of Dawud, and others. And the "Reminder" is meant to be the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab). Accordingly, the meaning is: "And We had indeed written in the revealed Books sent down to the prophets that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants, after We had written that in the Mother of the Book." This meaning is clear and free of difficulty. It has also been said that the Zabur in the verse is the Psalms of Dawud, and the Reminder is the Torah, and other things have been said. The most apparent of these is what we have mentioned, and it has been chosen by more than one scholar.

Know that we have already stated, in the introduction to this blessed book, that a verse may have two opinions among the scholars, both of which are true and are supported by the Qur'an. We will mention all of them, because all of it is truth that falls within the verse. Among these is this noble verse, because the meaning of "the earth" in His saying here, ﴿that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], has two possibilities according to the scholars:

The first: It is the earth of Paradise, which Allah will bequeath to His righteous servants on the Day of Resurrection. This view is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land, to dwell in Paradise wherever we will. And excellent is the reward of the workers"﴾ [az-Zumar: 74]. We have already discussed the meaning of their inheriting Paradise in full in Surat Maryam.

The second: The meaning of "the earth" is the land of the enemy, which Allah bequeaths to the believers in this world. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27]; His saying: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ to the end of the verse [al-A'raf: 137]; His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Musa said to his people, "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He causes to inherit it whom He wills of His servants, and the best outcome is for the righteous"﴾ [al-A'raf: 128]; His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, as He granted succession to those before them﴾ to the end of the verse [an-Nur: 55]; and His saying: ﴿So their Lord inspired to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them"﴾ [Ibrahim: 13-14], among other verses.

All the reciters except Hamza read the word "az-Zabur" with a fatha on the zay, and its meaning is "the Book." Hamza alone read "az-Zubur" with a damma on the zay. Al-Qurtubi said: "According to Hamza's reading, it is the plural of zubur." The apparent meaning is that he intends "az-Zibr" with a kasra, in the sense of "az-Zabur," i.e., "what is written." Accordingly, the meaning of Hamza's reading is: "And We had indeed written in the Books," and this supports that the meaning of "az-Zabur" in the fatha reading is the generic category of Books, not specifically the Psalms of Dawud, as we have explained. Hamza read "yarithuha ibadi" with a sukun on the ya', and the rest read it with a fatha on it.

God Almighty says: "Indeed, in this is a message (balaghan) for a people who worship" (Qur'an 21:106).

The demonstrative in His words "this" (hadha) [al-Anbiya: 106] refers to the Glorious Qur'an, of which this noble surah is a part. Al-balagh (a sufficiency, and that by which the desired aim is attained) means sufficiency and that by which one reaches one's goal. What He mentions here, that this Qur'an contains sufficiency for those who worship and that by it they attain their aim, i.e., the good of this world and the Hereafter, He mentions in another place, as in His words: "This is a message (balagh) for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is but one God, and that those of understanding may take heed" (Qur'an 14:52). He specified "the people who worship" with this because they are the ones who benefit from it.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, mentions that He did not send this Noble Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, to the creation except as a mercy to them, because he brought them that which makes them happy, and through which they attain every good of the worldly life and the Hereafter if they follow him. As for whoever opposes him and does not follow him, it is he who has deprived himself of his share of that great mercy. Some scholars have given an example for this. He said: If Allah caused a spring to gush forth for the creation, abundant in water and easy to draw from, so that people irrigated their crops and livestock with its water, and blessings followed them as a result, but some people remained negligent and lazy about working, and so they lost their share of that spring, then the gushing spring is itself a mercy from Allah and a blessing for both groups. But the lazy one is a calamity upon himself, since he has deprived himself of what would benefit him. This is clarified by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief and caused their people to settle in the abode of destruction?﴾ [Ibrahim: 28]. It has also been said: his being a mercy to the disbelievers is in that their punishment was delayed because of him, and they were secured by him from the punishment of total annihilation. But the first view is more apparent.

What Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in this noble verse, that He sent him only as a mercy to the worlds, indicates that he brought mercy to the creation through what this Great Qur'an contains. This meaning is clarified in several places in the Book of Allah, such as the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾ [al-Ankabut: 51], and His words: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86], to the end of the verse.

We have already presented the verses indicating this in Surat al-Kahf in two places of it. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, invoke curses upon the polytheists." He said: "Indeed I was not sent as one who curses, but I was sent only as a mercy."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 109:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you equally"﴾.

His saying ﴿Then if they turn away﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109] means: they turn away and avert from what you call them to. ﴿Then say: "I have announced to you equally"﴾ means: I have informed you that I am at war with you just as you are at war with me, and I am free of you just as you are free of me. This meaning indicated by this verse has been pointed to by other verses,

- such as His saying: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], meaning: let your knowledge and their knowledge of the annulment of the covenants be equal.

- And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my deed and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."﴾ [Yunus: 41]

- And His saying: "I have announced to you." Adhdhan (الأذان, announcement) means informing (al-i'lam). From it comes the adhan (call) to prayer.

- And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And an announcement from Allah﴾, the verse [al-Tawbah: 3], meaning: a notification from Him. His saying: ﴿Then be informed of a war from Allah﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 279], meaning: know. From it is the saying of (p-252) al-Harith ibn Hillizah:

؎"Asma' has announced to us her parting, and many a dweller whom the sojourn wearies"

meaning: she informed us of her parting.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 110:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and knows what you conceal﴾.

In this noble verse, He—majestic and exalted—mentions that He knows what His creatures utter aloud of speech, and He knows what they conceal. This meaning has been clarified in many verses,

• such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And conceal your speech or disclose it; indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Mulk: 13],

• and His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ [al-Nur: 29], in both places,

• and His saying: ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you disclose and what you were concealing"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16],

• and His saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 7],

and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 21, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾

The majority of the seven readers, other than Hafs from Asim, recited this word as qul rabbi (قُلْ رَبِّ), with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the lam, in the imperative form. Hafs alone recited it as qala rabbi (قالَ رَبِّ), with a fatha on the qaf and on the lam, with an alif between them, in the past tense. The reading of the majority indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say this. The reading of Hafs indicates that he carried out the command in action. What he was commanded to say here is what the Prophet of Allah, Shu'ayb, said, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], and his saying: "Iftah" (افْتَحْ), meaning: judge, as has already been explained.

* *

His saying: ﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 112], meaning: what you describe with your tongues of kinds of falsehood, by claiming partners and offspring for Him, and other things. As He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And their tongues describe the lie﴾ [al-Nahl: 62], the verse, and He said: ﴿And do not say, for what your tongues describe as falsehood﴾ [al-Nahl: 116], the verse. What the Prophet (ﷺ) said in this verse, Ya'qub said when he knew that his sons had done to their brother Yusuf something other than what they had told him. That is in His saying: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting. And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe"﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Al-musta'an means the one from whom help is sought. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

This is the end of the fourth part of this blessed book, and the fifth part follows it, God willing, and its beginning is Surah al-Hajj. Success is from Allah, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad and his family.
